news.title: Trump administration faces lawsuit over cancelled clean energy grants
news.text:
The Trump administration has acknowledged in a federal court filing that it recommended cancelling billions of dollars in clean energy grants based on the political identity of states, prompting criticism from Democratic lawmakers.

According to the filing, reported by The New York Times, the Department of Energy recommended ending more than 600 grants awarded in states won by Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and represented by two Democratic caucusing senators. 

The Office of Management and Budget later terminated 284 grants in October 2025.

In the 15 July filing, the Department of Energy said it "accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State."

The decision is being challenged in a class action lawsuit brought by a group of University of California researchers, who argue the grants were cancelled for political reasons.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer criticised the move, writing on X: "Trump admits he’s ripping the rug out from under hardworking families so he can get revenge on the Americans who didn’t vote for him. It’s sick and deranged."

The administration has not responded to the political criticism, while the legal challenge over the cancelled grants continues.

news.title: Trump administration admits it canceled grants from Harris voters
news.text:
July 25 (UPI) -- The Trump administration admitted that it canceled nearly $8 billion in grants slated for hundreds of clean energy projects "based solely" on whether a state voted for Kamala Harris for president, it was reported Friday.

In a recent court filing, a lawyer for the Energy Department said none of the axed projects lost their funding "based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor."

The Trump administration attorney added, "The 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing senators."

The government's admission, first reported by The New York Times, came out as part of a July 15 court filing in a class action lawsuit over the slashed grants.

The Department of Energy selected 600 grants for cancellation and sent the list to the Office of Management and Budget, which terminated 284 of them in October.

"Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda is being cancelled," OMB Director Russell Vought wrote on X.

Despite also being recommended for cancellation from energy officials, the OMB left untouched hundreds of projects in places that voted for Trump, court documents show.

"The inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state, i.e., whether the recipient's location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State," Trump administration lawyers wrote.

Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, called the move "unprecedented Trumpism and something we should never become numb to."

"Trump admits he's ripping the rug out from under hardworking families so he can get revenge on the Americans who didn't vote for him," the New York democrat added. "It's sick and deranged. His ego is so fragile, he'll punish families already struggling to put food on the table for a little bit of vengeance."

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said, "This mass partisan retribution is appalling, outrageous, dangerous, lawless, unconstitutional, unpatriotic and a massive offense against the Republic."

"Every elected official must denounce this imbecilic deep betrayal of America," Raskin added in a statement. "And the illegally impounded funds must be restored and released immediately to the blue states."
news.summary: The Trump administration admitted it canceled nearly $8 billion in grants "based solely" on whether a state voted for Kamala Harris for president.
news.author: Pedro Oliveira Jr

news.title: Homeless count leaves LA voters with impossible choice for mayor — and crisis for democracy
news.text:
Karen Bass is in deep trouble.

Her reelection bid was already shaky, thanks to lingering public outrage over the Palisades Fire.

Then she began losing staff, even after winning the primary election with a plurality of the vote. 

After longtime aide Doug Herman quit, she had to replace him with Julie Chávez Rodriguez, who managed Kamala Harris’s losing presidential campaign. 

Not exactly a hopeful sign.

But the mayor continued to argue that she had earned a second term, thanks to the progress that LA had made in reducing homelessness. 

Her campaign website boasted: “In the three years of the Bass Administration, LA has achieved its first-ever back-to-back decreases in homelessness.”

That argument is now toast.

On Friday, the LA Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) released its delayed homeless count for 2026.

It reported that the homeless population had risen almost 3.4% since 2025. And the number of “unsheltered” people living on the streets or in cars rose 7.9%.

That’s much worse than LA County, which recorded a 1.2% rise in homelessness and a 3.3% rise in the unsheltered population.

Bass tried to blame President Donald Trump. 

“The Trump Administration has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and rent — pushing more families to the edge — and slashed critical safety net funding,” her office claimed in a statement on Thursday.

Nobody’s fooled.

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

The city and LA County combined spend roughly $3 billion per year on homelessness. For that amount of money, LA should see dramatic progress, every year.

But instead of enforcing ordinances against homeless encampments, or addressing root causes like substance abuse and mental illness, the city invested in “housing first.”

Four walls do not solve the problem for people who pursue their cravings and their demons on the streets.

And LAHSA has been a disaster, with money flying out the door with little oversight or accountability. The city failed to monitor the agency and has been too slow in taking over its functions.

The homeless numbers are a major political problem for Bass. And under ordinary circumstances, the news should benefit Bass’s opponent in the general election, socialist City Council member Nithya Raman.

But there’s one problem: Raman chairs the City Council’s committee on homelessness. She is just as much to blame as the mayor.

If the homeless numbers had been available before the June 2 primary vote, it is possible that challenger Spencer Pratt would have qualified for the general election.

It does not seem that the homeless count was delayed for political reasons. Though it arrived later than expected, the homeless count has typically been delivered in late July.

Still, it would have been good for voters to know what was actually going on, as Mayor Bass claimed she had achieved great success.

“Los Angeles, we have been doing it for the last three years, and it’s the first time homelessness has gone down,” she declared during the televised mayoral debate.

Raman claimed that LA had made “incremental” progress, and introduced a new plan that, she said, would clear all of the homeless encampments by the end of her term.

Pratt cautioned against believing either of his two rivals on the homeless issue.

“This is an absolute failure for both of them,” he said. “They’re a team.”

Pratt, who lost his family home in the Palisades Fire, made homelessness a major focus of his campaign.

He drew attention to the issue on social media, and particularly to the abuse of animals within homeless encampments.

Pratt entered the election with tremendous momentum, and seemed to have finished in second place, until late ballots put Raman ahead of him, and into the general election.

In a further irony, Raman seemed to have benefited from a surge in LA neighborhoods with large numbers of homeless people. Critics suspect that she was boosted by ballot harvesting at homeless shelters.

So not only did Raman fail to improve homelessness, but she also may have benefited from that failure by using homeless votes to advance her campaign for mayor.

LA voters are left with a frustrating choice. On one hand, we can reelect a mayor who claimed to have improved homelessness, and failed. On the other hand, we can gamble on a radical politician whose socialist policies would arguably make the problem worse.

Voters should have had a real alternative. Spencer Pratt was that alternative. Now he is on the sidelines.

And thanks to California’s “jungle” primary system, there is no option for a write-in vote in the general election.

This is a crisis for local democracy. 

Leadership is going to have to come from somewhere. But it won’t be the mayor’s office.

Joel Pollak is Opinion editor of the California Post.
news.summary: Karen Bass is in deep trouble. Her reelection bid was already shaky, thanks to lingering public outrage over the Palisades Fire.
news.author: Joel Pollak

news.title: Troy Jackson secures Democratic nomination for Maine Senate race
news.text:
Maine Democrats officially have a new U.S. Senate nominee.

Troy Jackson, a veteran state politician and logger, secured the nomination Saturday at the party's state convention which was held weeks after the Democratic nominee Graham Platner bowed out due to mounting scandals.

Jackson, who secured 566 votes, defeated the only other candidate in the race, Sandra Pelletier, who received only five votes.

Taking the stage shortly after securing the nomination, Jackson said it was one of the "absolute honors" of his life to be named the Democratic nominee.

"So, I want you to hear this directly from me. There is a place in this campaign for all of you. There is work for you in this movement, and I will spend every day now through November earning that trust because today we turn the page," he said.

Jackson took aim at his opponent, incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and the Republican Party for the pain Americans feel economically right now.

He said he is running on protecting Social Security and Medicare, protecting abortion access, standing with the LGBTQ community and countering President Donald Trump's policies.

"Susan Collins keeps telling us everything is just fine, and they act like you know we're idiots," he said. "You know we all have eyes; we can see what's happening. We can see our paychecks and the bills that we have, and we know that we are getting screwed, and we also know who's to blame." 

"We cannot afford six more years of the same," Jackson said later on in his acceptance speech.

Jackson's solidification as the state's Democratic nominee comes after Platner withdrew from the race earlier this month following allegations of sexual assault by a former girlfriend, and a series of other controversies that have marred his campaign.

Platner has denied the sexual assault allegation.

At the start of the convention, Maine Democratic Party chair Charlie Dingman reflected on the moment that the state party found itself in and said he was proud of the work done to make the nominating process as transparent and representative as possible.

"The easy solution would have been to task a party committee with making that choice. Instead, instead, we responded to the growing grassroots movement in our state to build power for ordinary working people," he said.

Jackson will now officially take on Collins for control of Maine's Senate seat in November, a seat critical to Democrats' chances to regain control of the Senate.

But both candidates face their own challenges in their quest to win in November.

Although Collins has faced challengers in the past, this time she's running in a cycle where voters have soured on Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, and she's running in a state that was won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 by about 7 percentage points.

Jackson will have to build up his campaign and continue the momentum that was built around Platner with 101 days to go before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. He lost in the state's Democratic gubernatorial primary in June.

The nominee has also faced scrutiny for his past positions, as he always didn't support or vote for progressive issues.

When Jackson initially ran for public office in 2000, he did so as a Republican. Even after becoming a Democrat in 2004, he voted against same-sex marriage being legalized in 2009 and was against abortion rights when he was in the Maine State Senate.

Jackson has said since regretted his vote against same-sex marriage and has advocated for abortion access for years.
news.summary: Maine Democrats officially have a new U.S. Senate nominee. Troy Jackson, a veteran state politician and logger, secured the nomination Saturday.
news.author: Hannah Demissie

news.title: Maine Democrats pick Troy Jackson to replace Platner as Senate nominee
news.text:
BANGOR, Maine – With just over 100 days to go until the midterm elections, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson officially clinched the Democratic nomination for Senate at a party convention here Saturday, setting up a marquee fall matchup against longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. 

Jackson will replace Graham Platner, who withdrew as the nominee just over two weeks ago after an allegation of sexual assault, which he denies. 

“This process came together faster than any of us expected,” Jackson said in his victory speech before the gathered delegates and party officials at the Cross Insurance Center. “But this is important. The movement represented in this room did not just begin two weeks ago.”

Delegates picked Jackson over pharmaceutical executive Saundra Pelletier by a vote of 566-5 during a roughly two-and-a-half hour party convention that also served as a fall campaign kickoff for the state’s Democratic faithful.

“Power is never just given to working people. We have to band together and take it,” Jackson said earlier Saturday during his nominating address. “When the people in power refuse to listen, well, you have to organize. You have to stand together in solidarity together.”

“That’s how we took on the companies exploiting Maine loggers, and it's how we're going to take on Susan Collins,” he said. 

Jackson speaks during the nominating convention in Bangor, Maine, on Saturday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Jackson’s pick wraps up a chaotic few weeks for Maine Democrats, who had to convene Saturday’s convention to pick a new nominee ahead of a Monday deadline. They've been seeking to move on from Platner, who easily defeated Gov. Janet Mills in a primary last month with a populist message that resonated with Democratic voters despite a series of negative headlines that dogged his nearly yearlong campaign. 

Jackson, who unsuccessfully ran for governor this year, came into the convention as the prohibitive favorite after securing the support of a vast majority of delegates elected across the state’s counties last weekend to serve at the convention. 

Eve Breedlove, a young delegate from Penobscot County, said she’d supported Jackson in the gubernatorial race because of his support for progressive policies, which she said were similar to what Platner had campaigned on. 

“People still had that momentum behind him, and just with all of this happening, it’s unprecedented,” she said. “But in a way, I’m only 20 years old, so everything that’s ever happened in my life is very unprecedented."

Now, Democrats are looking ahead to November, when ousting Collins, the only Senate Republican to represent a seat carried by Kamala Harris in 2024, will be critical to their chances of flipping the chamber. Democratic delegates — many of whom said they’d known Jackson for years — called the new nominee an authentic candidate who would be a strong challenger to Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. 

“It’s going to be tough, but he’s got a real passionate support base,” said Melissa Smith, a Waldo County delegate who said she’d known Jackson for a decade. “People are tired of Susan Collins. She hasn’t done a town hall in what, 25, 30 years? The only way you can talk to Susan Collins is if you happen to run into her at the Hannaford [grocery store].”

Delegate Danielle Bailey cheers for Jackson during the nominating convention Saturday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A longtime state legislator, Jackson rose to serve as state Senate president for six years, leaving the role in 2024 due to term limits. A logger from northern Maine, his electoral career began in 2000, when he lost a race for the state House as a Republican before winning the seat as an independent two years later.

In 2004, he joined the Democratic Party and went on to serve in the state Senate from 2008 until 2014, when he left for an unsuccessful bid for Maine’s 2nd District. He returned to the chamber in 2016 for what would be an eight-year stint. 

Jackson finished in third place last month in Maine’s ranked choice Democratic primary for governor. 

His top competitors from that race, including Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and former state public health official Nirav Shah, revived their campaigns this month to seek the Senate nomination but dropped out last weekend after Jackson’s campaign said a majority of the delegates had pledged to support him. 

Jordan Wood, who lost the Democratic primary for the open 2nd District, and Dan Kleban, a founder of Maine Beer Company who briefly ran for Senate last year before endorsing Mills, were also among the candidates who entered the snap Senate primary before ending their campaigns and rallying around Jackson. 

Pelletier was the only other candidate who remained in the race through Saturday.

Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee to succeed retiring Rep. Jared Golden in the 2nd District, said Democrats running across the state were all focused on the issues motivating Maine voters. 

“What you’re seeing here is that that groundswell of energy that was really inspired by Platner’s campaign was really inspired by the same priorities that we’ve all been putting forward,” he said in an interview Saturday. 

In his remarks on Saturday morning, Jackson touted health care, union rights and a living wage for workers as top priorities. He also stressed his support for reproductive and LGBTQ rights, two key Democratic issues on which he held more conservative positions earlier in his career. 

He won big cheers in the convention hall Saturday as he spoke about his support for unions, which were critical in helping elect pro-Jackson delegates at the nominating meetings last weekend. 

Jackson arrives to speak at the nominating convention in Bangor on Saturday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Fall matchup

Democrats looking to flip the Senate — a prospect that looked unlikely a year ago — have expanded the map into red-leaning states ahead of the fall campaign, but Maine remains a top target. 

While national groups briefly appeared ready to step back from the race before Platner’s withdrawal, party leaders immediately endorsed Jackson on Saturday after publicly opting for a hands-off approach during the past few weeks. 

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand said Jackson had a “demonstrated ability to win.”

“A champion for affordable health care and working people, Jackson has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat Susan Collins, who is more vulnerable than she has ever been,” the two New Yorkers said in a joint statement. 

Jackson told reporters on Saturday that he had not yet spoken with Schumer. 

He enters the general election with a significant cash disparity against Collins, whose campaign ended June with $11 million on hand, according to her second-quarter federal filings. Jackson said he expected to have the resources to win “because we’ve got the right message.”

Affordable Maine, a Democratic advocacy group, on Friday released two new ads attacking Collins, one focused on a congressional stock trading ban and another on her vote to confirm Brett M. Kavanaugh, who was among the Supreme Court justices who voted to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. 

But Republicans appear ready to try to tie Jackson to Platner, and to highlight reports of his hot temper while serving in the state legislature. On Saturday, Republicans called him a "Democratic socialist” and an “ineffective legislator."

"Troy Jackson lost his bid to be governor and he will lose his bid to be senator. Jackson is a Democrat socialist who has only made life harder in Maine, while Susan Collins has secured $1.5 billion in funding to benefit Mainers in all 16 counties," Samantha Cantrell, a National Republican Senatorial Committee regional press secretary, said in a statement. 

Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC with ties to the chamber’s GOP leaders, launched a six-figure ad campaign Saturday focused on the reports about Jackson’s temperament as part of the $42 million the group has pledged to spend in Maine this year.

"Chuck Schumer forcefully removed Graham Platner from the ballot against the will of Maine voters, only to replace him with a deranged and scandal-plagued political insider,” SLF spokesman Chris Gustafson said in a statement. 

Jackson said Saturday that he anticipated the Republican attacks while acknowledging that he’d fought with people from both parties while in the legislature.

“I've cried on the Senate floor because I believe that people sent me to Augusta to deliver for them, and it's important to me,” he told reporters. “Anyone that I may have argued with, that I might have went too far and got too passionate, I apologize to. But I don’t have a problem with anyone in the legislature or in the U.S. Senate.”

Other Democrats sought to more subtly address those concerns. Charlotte Warren, a former mayor of Hallowell and onetime state legislator who reportedly clashed with Jackson in 2021, said he “wears his heart on his sleeve” as she formally nominated him at the convention.

“What I’ve learned about Troy in these moments: He listens. He works through disagreements, and when the fight is over he gets back to work for what he believes in, with the people he believes in,” she said.
news.author: Mary Ellen McIntire

news.title: Trump hits Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris with brutal one-two punch at White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner
news.text:
President Trump turned California’s two biggest Democratic stars into the punchline Friday night, unloading on Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris during a joke-filled White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner speech.

Trump mocked Newsom’s 2028 White House ambitions by claiming the governor had doomed himself with praise for Harris.

“Gavin Newsom has come out and said he will not be running for president, because nobody can say what he said about himself and survive,” Trump quipped. 

“Newsom was in big trouble when he openly admitted that Kamala was smarter than him,” he continued. “If Kamala is smarter than someone, you don’t want that person to be President of the United States of America.”

Trump has repeatedly used the line after the governor previously discussed his dyslexia and the challenges of reading from prepared remarks.

The jabs come as Harris has opened an early lead in the race for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. New polling shows the former vice president holds a significant advantage over Newsom and the rest of the field, leading by comfortable margins across the 14 most recent major polls.

Trump continued to tear into the California governor.

“I heard Gavin Newscum recently said we will lose our country if we don’t fight fire with fire,” Trump said before taking aim at Newsom’s handling of California’s devastating wildfires.

“To be fair, there’s only one thing we know about Gavin, and that’s that he definitely doesn’t want to fight fire with water.”

The president also blasted California’s policies, claiming the state is “enabling wildfires, paying drug addicts to be homeless, giving free sex changes to illegals, and telling rich people they’re going to take away, all your money is going to be taken away.”

The final remark referenced California’s controversial billionaire tax, which is set to appear on the November ballot.

“People are fleeing, they’re fleeing in droves and we can’t have that in this country,” Trump said.

The California Post reached out to both Harris and Newsom for comment.

Newsom’s office appeared to respond throughout Trump’s speech, posting three messages on social media that stated “Donald Trump is a son of a b—h,” “Donald Trump is a pig,” and an AI-generated image showing Trump looking into a mirror with the caption, “who’s the greatest slob of all.”Another post read, “Trump is cracking jokes about natural disasters while American families are still waiting for the disaster recovery dollars he promised.”

The correspondents’ dinner was the first since April’s event was disrupted by an assassination attempt on the president.

Trump also used his speech to mock the media and other political rivals.

“This place is really the largest group of Trump derangement syndrome people ever put together at one time,” he cracked.

Recalling last month’s cage fight outside the Oval Office, Trump joked, “Before I came along, if you wanted to see someone lose consciousness on the South Lawn of the White House, all you had to do is ask Joe Biden a question.”

He also took a shot at Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, saying he’d like to see the New York Democrat “have a rematch against an extremely simple question on a foreign policy from the Munich Security Conference,” referring to her widely criticized appearance at the event.
news.summary: "If Kamala is smarter than someone, you don't want that person to be President of the United States of America."
news.author: Titus Wu

news.title: ‘Like Graham Platner But Worse’: GOP Group Vows $42,000,000 Against Last-Minute Replacement Democrat
news.text:
A Republican group has vowed to spend at least $42 million against new Democratic Maine Senate nominee Troy Jackson, the Daily Caller News Foundation has learned. 

The Maine Democratic Party picked Jackson, a former logger and state senate president, at a Saturday convention to replace its former nominee Graham Platner, who had dropped out of the race after his ex-girlfriend accused him of rape. The same day, the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) announced it is spending $42 million on the race against Jackson — including a six-figure ad buy — and launched a 30-second ad stating that the new nominee is “worse” than the scandal-ridden man he replaced on the ballot. (RELATED: Now That Graham Platner Is Out, Here’s What Happens Next)“Chuck Schumer forcefully removed Graham Platner from the ballot against the will of Maine voters, only to replace him with a deranged and scandal-plagued political insider,” SLF Communications Director Chris Gustafson told the DCNF. “Mainers value steady leadership that yields real results for the Pine Tree State, making Susan Collins the clear choice once again this November.”

“Volatile personality. Anger issues with women. Verbal abuse,” states the voiceover of the SLF’s new ad obtained by the DCNF. The ad cited and quoted both a July 20 report from CNN and a July 21 report from The Hill.“It’s not Graham Platner, it’s Troy Jackson. Jackson has a history of conflicts with women, bullying, even intimidation. Jackson’s conduct was so bad his fellow Democrats raised alarm bells about his temperament,” the ad’s voiceover continues, citing other July reports. “Jackson is like Graham Platner but worse.”

The Republican super PAC’s ad also referenced a 2023 report from the Portland Press Herald stating an ethics panel was reviewing a complaint regarding Jackson’s second home. Some Republicans at the time said that the then-Senate president’s conduct may have amounted to mortgage fraud, according to the local Maine outlet.

SFL’s ad also cited the Bangor Daily News’ Wednesday report that Jackson owed $4,600 in back state taxes during his failed bid for Maine governor earlier this cycle.

“That’s the real Troy Jackson,” the voiceover concluded.

The northern Maine Democrat is set to face incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins, a moderate who has held the seat since 1997. Collins is the only remaining upper chamber Republican who represents a state former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024. The longtime GOP senator ended the second quarter of 2026 with $11 million on hand, the Maine Morning Star reported.

Jackson had come in third in Maine’s June 9 Democratic gubernatorial primary. His governor run was notably endorsed by both Platner and socialist Independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.

“Troy Jackson lost his bid to be Governor and he will lose his bid to be Senator,” National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) Regional Press Secretary Samantha Cantrell said in statement sent to the DCNF. “Jackson is a Democrat socialist who has only made life harder in Maine, while Susan Collins has secured $1.5 billion in funding to benefit Mainers in all 16 counties.”

We’re not from the left. We’re not from the right. We’re from the bottom, and we’re rising. In November, we will defeat Susan Collins. pic.twitter.com/Hg9sMnark3— Troy Jackson (@TroyJackson207) July 25, 2026

Platner had won the Democratic Senate primary, also held June 9, with over 70% of the vote against 78-year-old Gov. Janet Mills, who had already dropped out. Platner reported $1.7 million in cash on hand a little more than a week before he exited the race in disgrace, according to the Maine Morning Star.

The oyster farmer and Marine veteran’s landslide win came despite the fact that he had been embroiled in various scandals at the time including allegations of abuse by his ex-girlfriends, resurfaced incendiary Reddit posts and his decision to get a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol. Platner had been endorsed by many prominent left-wing figures including Sanders — who only withdrew his support after the Maine Democrat’s later rape allegation surfaced.

Jackson is widely viewed as being on the Democratic Party’s populist left flank like Platner and both men hold very similar views. Notably, both Jackson and Platner have used the word “genocide” to refer to Israel’s military actions in Gaza. However, Jackson had previously taken significantly more conservative positions, beginning his political career in the early 2000s as a Republican opposed to abortion and same-sex marriage. 

Jackson now supprorts a “federal right to abortion” and “comprehensive civil rights legislation protecting the LGBTQ+ community,” per his campaign website.

Affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, the SLF describes itself as “the only outside organization solely dedicated to protecting and expanding the Republican Senate Majority,” according to the Super PAC’s website.
news.summary: ‘Volatile personality. Anger issues with women’
news.author: Anthony Iafrate

news.title: Trump suggests LeBron James is ‘a racist’ in bizarre attack
news.text:
President Donald Trump suggested that basketball star LeBron James might be "a racist" during a White House news conference on Friday. 

Trump's remarks followed James's announcement that he would continue his NBA career by joining the Philadelphia 76ers. 

Trump was asked whether James, who publicly endorsed Kamala Harris for the 2024 presidential election, or Michael Jordan was the best-ever basketball player

“Michael Jordan is a guy that’s a friend of mine,” Trump said. “I play golf with him. He’s a really good guy. I think LeBron is, maybe he’s a racist, but maybe he doesn’t like Trump ... I would say Michael Jordan all the way.”

Trump had previously mocked James in 2020 after he campaigned for Joe Biden, prompting crowds at a rally in Pennsylvania to chant “LeBron James sucks”.

news.title: Nazi tattooed Graham Platner's behavior is turning voters OFF the Democratic Party
news.text:
One chaotic race for the US Senate could cost the Democrats the upper hand in the November midterm elections. 

By a two-to-one margin, voters say they are less likely to vote for a Democrat in the midterms due to the scandals surrounding Graham Platner, the Democrat who initially secured the party's nomination for the US Senate in Maine.

Platner dropped out of the race earlier this month after a slew of scandals, including allegations of sexual abuse and misconduct, contacting women outside of his marriage, and a prior revelation of having a Nazi tattoo.

Twenty-three percent of respondents to the latest Daily Mail/JL Partners poll say they are less likely to support Democrats, due to Platner's behavior, while 12 percent say they are more likely. 

But for most, it is not having an impact: 37 percent say there is no difference, 28 percent noted that they were unsure.

If Republicans hold the House and Senate in the midterms, the fallout could have have far reaching implications as Democratic presidential hopefuls like Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ro Khanna and Kamala Harris size up a 2028 run. 

Platner was backed by a slew of prominent Democrats in his race prior to the most disturbing round of allegations against him during which he was accused of sexual assault, a claim that added to an avalanche of prior controversies.

The new accusations were by far the most graphic and caused Platner's campaign to come tumbling down. 

In an 11-minute long video posted to social media in early July, he again denied the allegations but said that 'the immense amount of weight' on him forced him out of the race. 

He lost one endorsement after another, and national Democratic groups said that they would not invest any money into the race if he remained the nominee.

Congressman Ro Khanna of California posted noted on X at the time, 'I've been very clear that sexual assault or violence against women is a red line. These allegations are very serious and credible. Graham Platner should drop out from the race. I am withdrawing my endorsement.'

Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona shared, 'the allegations against Graham Platner are troubling and deeply serious. I am rescinding my endorsement.'

That prompted the party to hunt for a pick to replace him on the ballot.

Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, epidemiologist Nirav Shah, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, and former congressional candidate Jordan Wood were floated as potential picks to replace Platner. Jackson ended up being selected as the new nominee. 

One of of Platner's ex girlfriends Jenny Racicot, 41, told Politico earlier this month that she had an on-and-off relationship with Platner for more than two years before the night when he showed up to her rural Maine home uninvited in 2021.

Racicot, as well as fellow Platner ex Lindsey Fifield, sat down with CNN to discuss their alleged experiences with him as a partner as well.

She told Politico that she and Platner exchanged messages the night of the attack and she told him not to come over, but later that evening, she heard him letting himself into her unlocked house.

Platner came upstairs to where she was sitting on the couch and appeared to be 'blackout drunk' when he ignored her protests and started 'grabbing my pelvis and being really forceful of me.'

'I had been telling him these words, like: 'No, don't,'' she told Politico. 'And, the look on his face and realizing what was happening, I just realized that, like, I am in a situation where there's no consent here.'

Yet, the question of how he got so far permeated across the country. 

Platner faced numerous scandals since last fall, including the revelation of a Nazi tattoo that he has since covered up. 

Controversial Reddit posts also emerged during the course of the campaign, which Platner himself has described as including 'homophobic slurs, anti-LGBTQ+ jokes and sexually explicit stories denigrating gay men' to the Advocate last year.

Another recent controversy stemmed from revelations that Platner texted other women sexually while married, and the discovery of a shirtless profile on Kik.
news.summary: One chaotic race for the US Senate could cost the Democrats the upper hand in the November midterm elections.

news.title: There’s a Fake Rush Limbaugh Uploading New ‘Rush Hour’ Daily Podcasts on the Internet
news.text:
It’s a small YouTube account that hasn’t gotten much traction. At least not yet. Most of the episodes are still in double (or even single) digits of views/hits. But I’m fascinated by what it represents. It’s probably just a matter of time until it takes off. 

(Or gets banned.)

And if you’re a Rush Limbaugh superfan, you’ll probably find it a strange combination of awesome, heartwarming, dystopian, and creepy.

So very, very creepy.

“The Excellence in Podcasting Network” YouTube channel, starring “Rick LeBow,” has been uploading new daily episodes for a little over a month. Here’s a sample:

I’m 99.99% sure “Rick LeBow” is a fake name. It’s too on-the-nose. There’s a deceased Arkansas police sergeant by that name, an addiction counselor in Costa Rica, a doctor, and a few others, but nobody who’s ever worked in radio (as far as I can tell). And although he’s possibly a voice actor doing a Rush Limbaugh impression, the frequency of the updates — and the emotional flatness — points to AI.

Which, interestingly enough, is something we discussed two years ago:

In theory, it’d be wonderful for Rush Limbaugh to rise from the ashes and thrill his dittoheads one last time. And his fans would be beyond thrilled to hear his voice again — listening to his spin on Kamala Harris, the 2024 campaign, and the craziness of the world — and share the Limbaugh experience with our children and grandchildren. An AI version of Rush, done right, would be the ultimate tribute to America’s Truth Detector, our Doctor of Democracy, and America’s Anchorman: An ongoing legacy that continues to educate “young skulls full of mush” and promote the conservative beliefs that defined him.So as a fan, I’d loooove it if the EIB Network became the “AI” B Network and Rush roared again. His absence still hurts; the vacuum he left was never filled. But as a fan, I also suspect he wouldn’t support it. Rush Limbaugh would want us to think for ourselves. Rather than being pleased that we’re still turning to him for guidance, I think he’d be saddened. Rush championed the conservative principles of rugged individualism and self-determination, and asking an algorithm to speak for him — or think for us — is antithetical to the Limbaugh ethos.

My same teenage kid who alerted me to the Lego/Utah/Mormon YouTube controversy (and we’ll be updating that story soon) showed me this channel. I’m glad he did.

But I still don’t know if I like it.

On one hand, even a soulless, bloodless, AI-generated Rush Limbaugh facsimile is better than nothing. It’s a helluva nostalgia kick! For the most part, “Rick LeBow” nails Limbaugh’s personality and worldview: conservative, patriotic, optimistic, sincere. He’s still the same harmless, loveable fuzzball we know and love. (Or knew and loved.)

It made me realize how much I still miss him.

But on the other hand, it’s definitely not the real Rush Limbaugh. It’s just not. There’s a certain spark — that Limbaugh-esque twinkle-in-the-eye charm — that an AI impression lacks. It’s more like a tribute band than the genuine article.

And it’s almost certainly being done without the approval of the Limbaugh estate. That’s creepy, too. (And of dubious legality.)

Yet this is the wave of the future. The ubiquity of the technology guarantees it. As does its rate of improvement: AI keeps on getting better and better.

This is the worst it’ll ever be!

Two years ago, when I wrote about the possibility of Limbaugh’s legendary EIB network becoming the “AI” B network, a “new” George Carlin comedy concert, allegedly AI-created, had just dropped. (It’s since been scrubbed from the internet.)

Today, nobody is using two-year-old AI. It’s a dinosaur. The same technology that wowed us in 2024 has exponentially advanced. Had the Carlin estate not intervened, we could’ve had an endless stream of “new” George Carlin material that kept on getting funnier, wittier, and sharper. 

Imagine: Totally new, all-original comedy concerts every few months — and each one is better than the last!

That’s awfully enticing if you’re a Carlin fan.

But the Carlin estate did intervene. His daughter was especially offended:

My statement regarding the AI generated George Carlin special: My dad spent a lifetime perfecting his craft from his very human life, brain and imagination. No machine will ever replace his genius. These AI generated products are clever attempts at trying to recreate a mind…1/3— Kelly Carlin-McCall (@kelly_carlin) January 11, 2024

Politically, George Carlin and Rush Limbaugh were opposites. They didn’t agree on much.

But I suspect they’d agree on this.

Whether you applaud “Rick LeBow” or are repulsed by him, you ought to be aware of what he represents. He’s a small part of a much larger story.

One Last Thing: 2026 will reach a crescendo with the midterm elections. Nothing less than the fate of the America First movement teeters in the balance.

Never before have the political battle lines been so clearly defined. Win or lose, 2026 will transform our country.

That means: More stories, more videos, more content, more fun, more conservatism, more EVERYTHING!

news.title: Charli XCX erfindet sich neu
news.text:
Kürzlich sorgte Madonna für Spekulationen unter Fans, als sie auf Instagram schrieb: "If your Dance floor feels dead/ Maybe you're playing the wrong music". Auf Deutsch: "Wenn sich deine Tanzfläche tot anfühlt, spielst du vielleicht die falsche Musik". Sofort waren sich einige sicher: Die Sängerin, die gerade einen Nachfolger ihres gehypten Albums "Confessions on a Dance Floor" nachgelegt hat, teilt gegen Popstar-Kollegin Charli XCX aus, die zuvor in einem neuen Song den Tod des "Dancefloors" ausgerufen hatte.

Doch ob Madonna nun wirklich auf die britische Sängerin angespielt hat oder nicht: Charli XCX dürften solche Gerüchte vermutlich sogar in die Karten spielen. Es gibt wohl kaum einen Popstar, der das Spiel von Selbstinszenierung zwischen Internet-Hype, Ironie und künstlerischem Anspruch so beherrscht wie die 33-Jährige.

Mit "Brat" hat Charli XCX einen Sommer lang die Pop- und Internetkultur geprägt. Gleichzeitig wirkt sie mit ihrer coolen Art manchmal wie ein Anti-Popstar fernab des Hochglanz-Glamours à la Taylor Swift. Sie inszeniert sich als exzessives Partygirl, kommentiert dieses Image aber immer wieder auf einer Meta-Ebene selbst, hat sogar in einem Film darüber mitgespielt.

Jetzt hat die Sängerin also ihre neue Platte herausgebracht. Passenderweise versammelt sie auf dem Albumcover den Musiker John Cale, Designer Marc Jacobs und Regie-Größe Martin Scorsese, wohl eine Anspielung auf ihre Interessen fernab der Popmusik. 

Das überrascht nicht. Es reiht sich ein in eine Gewohnheit der Sängerin, ihren Sound neu zu erfinden. Der "Spiegel" schrieb vor zwei Jahren, Charli XCX sei seit dem Anfang ihrer Karriere das "menschgewordene Internet", sie beherrsche die Kunst, "das Netz ins echte Leben zu übersetzen und für sich zu nutzen".

Wie sehr das zutrifft, zeigte der Trubel rund um das "Brat"-Album. Die Britin, die mit dem Schlagzeuger George Daniel der Band The 1975 verheiratet ist, hatte damals mit dem Titel ihres sechsten Studioalbums einen Trend ausgelöst.

"Brat" bedeutet so viel wie "Göre". Die Idee dahinter: Machen, was man will, egal, was andere denken. Eine Art Gegentrend zur übertriebenen "Clean-Girl-Ästhetik". In einem BBC-Interview sagte sie dazu, man brauche eigentlich nur ein Top ohne BH, ein Feuerzeug und eine Packung Zigaretten, um "Brat" zu sein.

Der Begriff wurde in ihrer Heimat Großbritannien damals vom Collins Dictionary zum Wort des Jahres gekürt. Das giftgrüne Cover wurde zum Vorbild für Memes und Mode. Sogar das Team um die damalige US-Präsidentschaftskandidatin Kamala Harris sprang auf die virale Welle auf.

Natürlich hätte Charli XCX, die mit bürgerlichem Namen Charlotte Emma Aitchison heißt, den "Brat"-Sommer einfach noch weiter laufen lassen können. Stattdessen inszenierte sie das Ende des Hypes gleich selbst. In der selbstironischen Satire "The Moment", in der sie eine überzeichnete Version von sich spielt, erklärte sie "Brat" dieses Jahr für beendet. Dem "Rolling Stone"-Magazin sagte sie, es sei für sie kreativ nicht befriedigend, zweimal dasselbe zu machen. "Alle meine Alben spielen mit Gegensätzen". Sie stünden im Widerspruch zueinander. Genau das sei das verbindende Element.

"Music, Fashion, Film" steht aber mit elf Songs inhaltlich nicht unbedingt im Widerspruch zum Vorgänger, es ist eher eine Reflexion über den "Brat"-Hype und stellt die Frage: Wer ist Charli XCX eigentlich wirklich? Im Song "I'm Afraid" thematisiert sie ihre Unsicherheiten und ihre Angst vor dem Scheitern als Künstlerin und Ehefrau. In "Camera" fragt sie sich, ob sie überhaupt Musik machen möchte und sie "dumm" ist, wenn sie mit bald 34 Jahren versucht, Schauspielerin zu werden. Doch es gibt auch wieder selbstironische Brüche. In dem eingängigsten Song des Albums "Wink Wink" verspricht die Musikerin mit einem Augenzwinkern, kein "bad girl" mehr zu sein und spielt auf ihr "Brat"-Partygirl-Image an.

Zwar erklärte die Sängerin im "Rolling Stone"-Interview, sie habe nie behauptet, ein Rockalbum zu machen, dennoch bringt die neue Platte unbestreitbar einen rockigen Sound mit Drums und verzerrten Gitarren mit. Wie zum Beispiel "Rock Music", jener Song, der auch Madonnas Instagram-Post inspiriert haben könnte. Das Musikvideo spielt mit Rock-'n'-Roll-Klischees. Charli XCX wirft etwa einen Fernseher aus dem Fenster.

Dort beschwört sie auch das Ende der Tanzfläche: "I think the dance floor is dead/ So now we're making rock music" ("Ich denke, die Tanzfläche ist tot, also machen wir jetzt Rockmusik"). Dem "Rolling Stone" sagte sie, die viel diskutierte Zeile befasse sich sehr viel mit ihrer Beziehung zu "Brat" und ihrer persönlichen Erfahrung mit dem Album, sei aber nicht als Kritik an Dance-Musik gemeint.

Der Albumtitel "Music, Fashion, Film" klingt jedenfalls wie eine Art Selbstporträt und beschreibt ziemlich treffend das, was die Künstlerin abseits ihrer Musik interessant macht. Sie ist nicht nur eine versierte Songwriterin, die unter anderem Songs für Camila Cabello und Selena Gomez geschrieben hat oder den Soundtrack zum Film "Wuthering Heights" beisteuerte. Sie ist auch leidenschaftliche Cineastin, etwa ein Fan des deutschen Filmemachers Werner Herzog und aktive Nutzerin der Plattform Letterboxd, bei der man Filme bewerten kann. Beim Thema Mode redet sie ebenfalls gerne mit. Ihre eigenwilligen, edgy Outfits sind für viele ein Stil-Vorbild.

Apropos Mode: Die Gerüchte um einen Streit zwischen dem Popstar und Madonna haben sich übrigens wieder erledigt. Bei einer Modenschau bei der Paris Fashion Week saßen die beiden nebeneinander - und umarmten sich herzlich.

(Von Sabrina Szameitat/dpa)

news.title: ‘Maybe he's a ‌racist', President Trump takes swipe at LeBron James
news.text:
‘Maybe he's a ‌racist', President Trump takes swipe at LeBron James

President Donald Trump, asked to weigh in on the basketball careers of Michael Jordan and LeBron James, said that James might be a racist.

In a White House press conference, Fox News' Peter Doocy mentioned the Friday news that James intends to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers, then asked the president whether Jordan or James is the "best ever."

Trump replied, "Michael Jordan is a guy that's a friend of mine. I play golf with him. He's a really good guy. I think LeBron is - maybe he's a racist, but maybe he doesn't like Trump. I don't know. I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way."

James endorsed the three candidates that ran against Trump in the past three presidential elections: Hillary Clinton in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024.

James also criticised Trump following the president's withdrawal of the Warriors' invitation to the White House in 2017, after Golden State star Stephen Curry stated that he would have declined the visit.

Jordan, 63, won six NBA titles for the Chicago Bulls in the 1990s and was a five-time league MVP.

James, 41, owns four NBA championship rings and has been selected MVP four times during his career with the Cleveland Cavaliers, Miami Heat and Los Angeles Lakers. He is the NBA's all-time leader in points and games played.

news.title: In Michigan, the price of energy is on the ballot and both parties know it
news.text:
Christine Waugh-Fleischmann, an art teacher who said she spends up to $200 a week on gas driving to see her grandchildren, is a Democratic voter in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District. One of the most competitive seats in the country, it is currently held by Republican Representative Tom Barrett and she believes the seat can be flipped, partly due to the high price of gas. 

“I do see a lot of people in my conservative neighborhood here who are very upset,” she told Reuters. “It’s gas. It’s grocery prices, it’s health care costs.”

The arithmetic of her frustration is easy to trace. After war broke out with Iran in late February, the average price of gas in Michigan jumped roughly 32 percent in three weeks, from $2.99 to $3.95 a gallon. Governor Gretchen Whitmer declared a formal energy emergency to let southeast Michigan stations sell cheaper summer-blend fuel, citing both the war and tariffs. Prices kept climbing anyway — including a 90-cent spike in a single week, among the sharpest in any midterm battleground — briefly topping $4 before coming down in recent months.

Crisis, emergency orders, persistent pain heading into the fall: That is the narrative spine of Michigan’s midterms, and both parties know it.

A ground shift

Republicans spent years circling Michigan as their best 2026 pickup opportunity. Now doubts are creeping in. A Democrat won a special state Senate election in May by nearly 20 points in a district Kamala Harris carried by less than one, and President Donald Trump’s economic approval fell even among Republicans, from 74 percent to 62 percent, between March and April.

In a Climate Power survey of 600 likely Michigan voters conducted in mid-June, 42 percent of those polled, including 44 percent of independents, said they would be less likely to vote for a congressional candidate who supports Trump’s energy policies, as opposed to 21 percent who said they’d be more likely. And 58 percent said Trump has made energy prices more expensive, while 63 percent rejected his claim that high gas prices are a “small price to pay” for the war in Iran. Since the war began, 45 percent said they had grown more supportive of diversifying America’s energy sources, including solar and wind.

“Trump’s energy agenda is costing Michigan families at the pump and on their power bills — and voters know it,” said Tom Lenard, Climate Power’s Michigan director, warning that candidates who back it “do so at their own political peril.”

Not every voter in Barrett’s district sees it that way. Alexander Melton, a 38-year-old heating and air conditioning technician, told Reuters that he still backs the Republican congressman. “We don’t dictate the price of gas,” he said.

Affordability versus the ‘Green New Scam’

In the Democratic Senate primary, which takes place August 4, Haley Stevens, Mallory McMorrow, and Abdul El-Sayed have all tied affordability messaging to clean energy — McMorrow, before exiting the race, called it “a freedom issue, it’s a cost issue” and argued that Democrats are “on the precipice” of lowering bills. Republican Mike Rogers, who’s running for a U.S. Senate seat for the second time, countered that the push for renewables is itself what is driving up Michigan’s energy costs.

Underneath the messaging war sits real economic damage. Michigan lost $4.1 billion in planned clean manufacturing investment and roughly 11,700 jobs after the Trump-era rollbacks, while $540 million in climate grants were canceled or delayed — including $156 million meant to help low-income residents install solar panels. And the administration ordered Consumers Energy to keep the J.H. Campbell coal plant running past its planned retirement, a move the state’s attorney general and other critics said will cost ratepayers more than transitioning away from it.

The fallout has cut across party lines. In March of last year, Representative John James of Shelby Township and at least seven other House Republicans called on their colleagues to preserve the Biden-era clean energy tax credits. “We must not neglect the sector-wide energy tax provisions that manufacturers and job creators rely on in my district,” James said.

Divided government, divided stakes

The starkest fight is in Lansing. Michigan’s 2023 Clean Energy and Jobs Act requires 100 percent renewable electricity by 2040, but the November elections could determine the law’s future. House Republicans last month passed “Project Lighthouse,” a package that would repeal the clean energy mandates; its sponsor, state Representative Pauline Wendzel, called the 2023 requirements “arbitrary” and said they help large investor-owned utilities instead of everyday ratepayers. The legislation is likely dead in the Democratic-held Senate — for now. But DTE Energy and Consumers Energy, the state’s largest utilities, will submit integrated resource plans in 2026 for the first time under the new law, meaning the election will set the ground rules just as they take effect.

Ben Poulson, state government affairs director for the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, argued the repeal legislation reaches further than its sponsors let on. “It repeals a lot of programs that we have been using to lower energy waste and lessens the accountability that we have on utility companies here in the state,” he told Planet Detroit.

Denise Keele, executive director of the Michigan Climate Action Network, said that climate change is showing up on the campaign trail under a different name. “We’re seeing it show up as energy affordability,” she said, noting that Michiganders pay some of the highest residential electricity and gas rates in the country. House Republicans, she said, “are essentially blaming clean and renewable energy as [to] why those energy prices are going up” — even though renewables make up only about 11 percent of the state’s mix and wind and solar are cheaper and faster to build. Her frustration cuts both ways: Not enough Democrats, she argued, are running on renewable energy’s success, a reticence she likened to what acclaimed environmental activist and journalist Bill McKibben calls “climate hushing.” The honest case — that prices will rise less with renewables than with fossil fuels — “is apparently too hard to message.”

Data centers and utility money

The hottest flashpoint may be data centers, which have driven up utility rates while promising jobs — and split traditional Democratic constituencies. Gubernatorial frontrunner Jocelyn Benson, endorsed by the Michigan League of Conservation Voters at a Grand Rapids riverfront event, has pledged enforceable guardrails on data centers and utilities and a moratorium on companies that violate environmental standards. Her platform centers on expanding clean energy to lower utility bills, replacing aging water infrastructure and reinstating polluter pay laws. 

But some unions back the data center projects. “We respectfully urge policymakers to support a responsible path forward for data center development that protects communities, grows the tax base, strengthens our workforce and keeps Michigan competitive for decades to come,” Douglas W. Stockwell, business manager and general vice president of Operating Engineers 324, testified at a hearing in Michigan’s House of Representatives.

Voter anger at the utilities is reshaping the money race, too. More than 150 Michigan politicians from both parties have pledged to reject campaign funding from Consumers Energy and DTE, according to the Michigan League of Conservation Voters — even as Consumers Energy requested another rate hike for its electricity customers this week. 

“This is disgusting what’s happening and it’s exploitative, it’s extractive, it’s unethical,” said Jerry Norris, a Lansing community activist who said he is following the money this cycle. “It might not own everybody when they accept money like that, but it influences it, and it creates an obligation and it creates a debt,” he told WILX10.

For voters like Alexis Jones of Lansing, the debate comes down to a number on an envelope. His utility bill is “almost $400,” he said. 

“It’s terrible. And not only do I have to look out for me, but I’ve got little munchkins, grandkids, to look after. And things are out of control.”

news.title: Trump Admin Admits It Canceled Clean Energy Funding Only for Blue States
news.text:
If there’s one unifying principle that unites the entire, sprawling federal government apparatus during the second Trump administration, then surely it is the fact that every department and every agency, on all levels, has seemingly been instructed to go about their business with the most petty vindictiveness possible. If you’re not doing the stated job of your department without also inflicting some kind of punishment on half of the country because they dared to participate in the democratic process and vote in 2020 and 2024, then by god, you are doing it wrong in the eyes of the President, and when he hears about it, you’re going to be shown the door and replaced by someone who will continue hurting the correct people. The latest department to admit as much in court filings? That would be the Department of Energy, which stated on the record that the hundreds of clean energy grants it canceled, worth billions of dollars, were “based solely” on whether the states those projects were in had voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

That’s it. That’s the entire criteria that went into determining which billions of dollars in grants were cut or withdrawn, and which ones remained–“which ones remained” being a status that can also be expressed as “all of the clean energy projects that happened to be located in red states.” Those solar, wind, hydro projects, etc., were found to be worthy of the continued funding. Weird!

NEW: In a stunning admission, the Trump administration admitted in court documents that it canceled billions in energy grants to states “based solely” on politics — and whether that state was represented by Democrats and backed Harris in 2024. 
www.nytimes.com/2026/07/24/b… 

— tony romm (@tonyromm.bsky.social) 2:10 PM · Jul 24, 2026

Ironically, this actually ended up being much less grant slashing than Trump’s own Department of Energy had recommended. After being tasked to review its spending, the DoE created a list of recommended projects to cancel of more than 600 grants that had been awarded by the Biden administration for all sorts of clean energy projects, in all 50 states, regardless of political alignment. However, when it came time to announce the cuts, the White House budget office announced only 284 of the grants totaling nearly $8 billion were being terminated. The criteria: Every single grant from a blue state, none of the grants from red states. The White House’s spokesman victoriously claimed that the administration was clashing “Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda,” but failed to mention that it would be preserving all of that “Green New Scam” funding to projects located in any state that had voted for Donald Trump in 2024. Obviously, this is because the White House did not want to be seen stripping investment and jobs from those states, because it trusts that red state voters not only do not care if the administration wantonly punishes blue states, but that its MAGA supporters actively want to see every resident of states like California, Illinois or Colorado hurt as much as possible.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright, meanwhile, lied and swore through his teeth in a June House of Representatives hearing that none of the canceled grants had been politically motivated. As he put it: “No decisions were made on politics. I keep hearing that charge. It’s bullshit. We’re going to say it a million times.”

Except, whoops: Officials and attorneys of Wright’s own department admitted in more recent court filings, in response to a lawsuit from California researchers challenging their loss of funding, that politics was the sole, exclusive reason for why funding was stripped from every single one of these projects. As a Department of Energy lawyer put it in a court filing in July: “With one exception, the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing senators.” The attorney likewise admitted that the grant terminations had not been “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor.”

That leaves: Pure, petty punishment! Other agencies have revealed, meanwhile, that they also determined which of their grants to terminate by using methods as broad as searching for specific keywords that smacked of “DEI” and other Trump admin catchphrases.

The smell of authoritarianism. 
The WH used keyword searches (related to diversity & gender) to review $2B worth of federal grants & illegally terminated them w/o real cause. It was based on political alignment.
This is a violation of the 1st Amendment.🧵
🧪 apnews.com/article/cali…

— Princess Vimentin PhD | Cancer Biologist (@princess-vimentin.bsky.social) 3:08 PM · Jul 22, 2026

This is of course nothing new for the broader Trump administration, which has taken unequal treatment of the states to entirely new heights during his second term in office. Trump is personally approving FEMA deployments, for instance, withholding disaster aid from blue states even when they suffer far more damage in the same storm as a neighboring red state. A detail I love: The Trump-appointed official who made waves earlier this year by claiming he could see ghosts and teleport to Waffle House locations was not in fact the one denying aid to states in need, but was generally considered by his FEMA colleagues to be an effective administrator even though he was also a crazy person. Just last week, meanwhile, we’re seeing another disproportionate response, as the administration is howling over New Jersey’s admission that a technical error resulted in it registering thousands of ineligible people to vote, when the same administration ignored the same type of clerical error when it happened earlier this year in red Texas.

The message could scarcely be more clear: If you live in a state that did not vote for Donald Trump, then the federal government does not recognize that you are worthy of its services. It doesn’t matter if you’re one of the many millions of Republicans who happens to live in New York, Massachusetts or Oregon–in that case, you’re just collateral who deserves to be denied clean energy investment or disaster aid by association. That’s what you get, for living somewhat near a person who voted for Kamala Harris!

“The risk that the Trump administration is willing to go to extreme lengths to politicize grant-making is not a hypothetical,” said Devin O’Connor of the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. “If they are willing to be that blatant about it, then I think we should take seriously when they put forward a framework that would allow for the extreme politicization of grant-making across all of the federal government.”

news.title: Staff turnover is rampant under Trump 2.0 – with insidious results | Arwa Mahdawi
news.text:
Donald Trump loves a construction project. He’s building a ballroom, revamping a reflecting pool, and overseeing the construction of a skyline-altering arch in Washington DC. For his next real estate scheme, may I suggest a giant revolving door in the White House? It would certainly get a lot of use: senior officials are leaving Trump’s second administration at record rates.

According to a new report called Quiet Chaos by the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, 27 Senate-confirmed officials have left their positions within cabinet departments to date. That’s nearly 150% higher than the 11 departures in the first 18 months of Trump’s first administration. Per the report, it is also “nearly two and a half times as many as Trump’s first administration (11) and over six times as many as the average between the George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations (4.3)”.

High-profile departures, like that of homeland security secretary Kristi Noem’s, have had a lot of media coverage. But as the Partnership for Public Service note in their report, there has been “remarkably little public attention” when it comes to overall departures in Trump 2.0. Indeed, the narrative has largely been that while Trump’s first term was a chaotic mess marked by constant personnel changes, his second presidency has been far more stable.

And that narrative isn’t entirely wrong. In Trump’s first term the rapid turnover was a sign that the reality TV host and real estate nepo baby had no idea what he was doing. In Trump 2.0, however, the departures point to something far more insidious. Rather than signaling incompetence, they are fuelinga power grab by a president who seems to think of himself as a king.

“Turnover on this scale does not just thin the government’s leadership ranks – it concentrates power in the president,” Chris Piper from the Partnership for Public Service writes in a blog post. “Each seat left to an acting official is one the president can fill on his own terms without the Senate’s advice and consent: no vetting, no confirmation hearing, no vote.”

Trump himself has said he likes acting officials because the temporary nature of the position gives him more control. “And so, Acting gives you much greater flexibility,” the president said in his first term. “A lot easier to do things.” Last month Trump similarly told the Wall Street Journal that he thought the non-permanent status of Bill Pulte, his incoming acting director of national intelligence and a man sometimes referred to as “Little Trump”, was an asset. “You’re less shackled,” he said. “It sort of gives you more power, you know, for a somewhat limited period of time.”

Power, and the rapid accretion of it in the executive branch, is the overwhelming theme of Trump’s second term. The conservative supermajority in the supreme court, which Trump helped create, has been invaluable to him in this regard. In July 2024, the court ruled that former presidents are entitled to some degree of immunity from criminal prosecution, nullifying the chance of an election subversion case against him before the election. Then, last month, the supreme court gave the president another gift: the power to fire leaders of independent agencies or commissions. The decision in Trump v Slaughter overturned Humphrey’s Executor, a 1935 ruling that the US constitution did not grant “illimitable power of removal” to the president.

Trump doesn’t quite have carte blanche to remove whomever he likes. On the same day as that decision, the supreme court ruled in Trump v Cook that the Federal Reserve was an exception to Trump’s power. Nevertheless, it is hard to overstate the significance of the Slaughter ruling, which upended almost a century of well-settled law curbing executive power. “Today, the court discards that democratic regime in favor of one that distorts the structure of government to fit the majority’s theory of unitary, total executive control. The result is a president who emerges with far greater power than ever before,” justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote in her dissent. Trump, meanwhile, wrote on Truth Social that it was “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years”.

I highly doubt that Trump has spent significant portions of his life thinking about the constitutionality of the Humphrey’s Executor decision. But do you know who has? The people at the Heritage Foundation, who are behind Project 2025, which is widely seen as the playbook for Trump’s second term. Overturning Humphrey’s Executor is right there on page 560 of Project 2025. Also in that playbook are steps to interfere with election administration and weaponize the Department of Justice against election officials who make decisions the Trump administration disagrees with. In other words: a strategy for influencing the upcoming election. Make no mistake: the masterminds behind Trump’s second term haven’t overseen “the Greatest Increase in Presidential Power in the last 100 years” just to easily cede that power to a Democratic president at the next election.

news.title: Maine Democrats to nominate Troy Jackson to replace Platner in US Senate race
news.text:
WASHINGTON, July 25 - Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson is poised to accept the Democratic Party's U.S. Senate nomination on Saturday, formally ending the two-week scramble to replace Graham Platner on the ballot for November's midterm election.

Platner withdrew on July 10 after sexual assault allegations, which he denies.

Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former Republican from northern Maine, locked up the nomination last weekend, when his supporters dominated the state party's delegate selection process. Jackson's top rivals suspended their campaigns after his decisive showing.

Donations from nearly 25,000 supporters flooded the presumptive nominee's campaign coffers with upwards of $600,000 between Sunday and Wednesday. Jackson's campaign said on Wednesday it had raised more than $1 million since he jumped into the truncated race earlier this month.

Some 600 delegates will select the nominee at a party convention in Bangor. Jackson and Saundra Pelletier, the wealthy chief executive of a biopharmaceutical company, are the only remaining candidates in a race that had ballooned to a field of 13.

MAINE RACE CRUCIAL FOR SENATE

Jackson's acceptance will kick off a 101-day sprint to unseat five-term Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable Republican who has used her seniority and perch as Senate Appropriations Committee chair to steer resources to Maine.

Collins is the only Republican up for reelection in a state that Democrat Kamala Harris won in 2024, making Maine a top flip opportunity for Democrats hoping to regain control of the chamber for the final two years of President Donald Trump's administration.

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but winning Maine is crucial to both parties' midterm strategies. Victory for Republicans would shrink Democrats' path to a majority, while a Democratic upset would support the party's bid for control.

Jackson held a narrow lead over Collins among likely general election voters in a University of New Hampshire poll released this week.

Collins, a 73-year-old moderate with an $11 million war chest, was last reelected in 2020. She won by nearly 9 percentage points, even as Mainers backed Democrat Joe Biden over Trump by a similar margin. Harris, herself a replacement nominee after Biden abruptly withdrew, carried Maine by about 7 percentage points.

Experts say affordability, Trump and immigration are likely to be key issues in the general election. Jackson has called for abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, an agency that has killed several people in high-profile incidents this year, including a 26-year-old Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13.

Collins voted for $70 billion in immigration enforcement funding without ICE reforms last month but has called for a pause in the agency's traffic stops. Trump has since said such stops must continue, describing them as one of the agency's most important and effective tools.

Social issues will also likely surface in the contest between Collins and Jackson. Jackson now supports abortion rights and same-sex marriage but opposed both in his state legislative career until his second Senate term in 2016.

His anti-abortion Senate voting record was raised in ads against him during his unsuccessful run in Maine's gubernatorial primary this year.

While it's unclear whether Republicans will invest in similar advertising in the Collins race, Republican officials say his past position leaves Collins less vulnerable over her vote to put Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court, which led to the overturning of federal abortion rights. REUTERS

news.title: Donald Trump says LeBron James might be ‘a racist’ and labels Michael Jordan greatest ever
news.text:
Donald Trump said LeBron James might be “a racist” during a news conference at the White House on Friday.

Trump was speaking hours after James confirmed his career will continue with a move to the Philadelphia 76ers. The 41-year-old had been considering his retirement from the NBA after playing his last game for the LA Lakers following eight seasons.

Trump was asked who was the best ever basketball player between Michael Jordan and James, a staunch critic of Trump’s presidency.

“Michael Jordan is a guy that’s a friend of mine,” Trump said. “I play golf with him. He’s a really good guy. I think LeBron is, maybe he’s a racist, but maybe he doesn’t like Trump. I don’t know. I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way.”

James has not responded to the comment.

The six foot nine inch James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, began his illustrious career with Cleveland, twice winning the championship with Miami before returning to the Cavaliers to claim a third and adding a fourth with the Lakers.

His four titles and four MVP awards trail Jordan’s six titles and five MVP awards.

James publicly endorsed Trump’s rival candidate Kamala Harris in the 2024 US presidential election. In a message posted to social media, the 39-year-old Los Angeles Lakers star wrote: “What are we even talking about here?? When I think about my kids and my family and how they will grow up, the choice is clear to me. VOTE KAMALA HARRIS!!!”

The post also included a video featuring clips of racist remarks made by Trump and comedian Tony Hinchcliffe, ending with the caption: “Hate takes us back.”

In 2020, Republican candidate Trump mocked James after he campaigned for President Joe Biden. At a rally in Pennsylvania, Trump said he “felt badly” for James – who had just won his fourth NBA Championship – because Finals ratings were considerably down.

He added: “I didn’t watch one shot. I get bored.”

The crowd then erupted into chants of “LeBron James sucks,” to which Trump responded: “What a crowd!”

Jordan was forced to deny he had endorsed Trump response, after fake social media posts suggested he had taken sides.

In a statement to The Independent, Jordan’s representatives strenuously denied that the basketball icon had endorsed either candidate leading up to the election. “There is absolutely no truth to the claim that Michael Jordan has made an endorsement in the presidential election,” they said. 

James has decided to join the Sixers, reportedly on a two-year deal worth around £6m.

In a series of posts on his official X account, the four-times NBA champion said as he prepares to embark upon a 24th campaign: “I thought I was done when the season ended. I wasn’t ready to announce it, and I knew I needed some time to really decide, but I was pretty sure I played my last game.

“I was honest at that last press conference when I said I needed to look at myself and decide if I still love this game. I still truly love this game, and I have more to give.

“The last few weeks have really been special. I’ve never been able to have no clue what to do and take real time to just think. I’ve had an incredible few months with all the people I love trying to figure it all out.

“This is my last decision. I’m not going for money. I’m not going for family. What am I really playing for at this point? I still want to sacrifice. I still want to work. I still want to grind. I still want to compete, to win and to have a chance at the feeling of winning another championship.

“I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time.

“Thank you LA. Miami, I’ll forever love and north-east Ohio will always (be) home!”
news.summary: LeBron James is a staunch critic of Donald Trump and the president appears to have taken it personally
