news.title: Democrats in Maine gather to replace Graham Platner in the race against Susan Collins
news.text:
Democrats are gathering in Bangor, Maine, on Saturday to formally nominate a new candidate for U.S. Senate, as the party looks to move past the scandal-plagued campaign of Graham Platner and refocus its sights on unseating longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins.

It's a Senate matchup with far-reaching political implications. Democrats need to net a total of four seats to win back control of the chamber this fall, and party officials see the contest in Maine as one of their best opportunities.

The race was thrown into turmoil earlier this month when Platner, the party's initial nominee, ended his campaign after a woman he previously dated came forward and accused him of raping her in 2021. Platner has denied the allegation, but it was the final straw for Democrats after months of controversy surrounding him. 

Now, after an abbreviated and chaotic search for a replacement, Maine Democrats are hoping to rally behind a new candidate who can harness the same energy and momentum of the Platner campaign.

The apparent front-runner heading into Saturday's convention is Troy Jackson. The former president of the Maine Senate has already garnered support from the bulk of elected delegates who will cast ballots for the nominee, and nearly every one of his primary rivals has dropped out of the race.

Maintaining Platner's movement, without the baggage 

Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from northern Maine, is running on an economic populist message that mirrors much of what Platner emphasized in his campaign, rejecting the Democratic establishment and focusing on affordability concerns, backing policies like Medicare for All and raising taxes on the ultra-wealthy and large corporations.

Like other more progressive candidates on the left, Jackson is pushing for the abolishment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and an end to U.S. military aid to Israel. He's also advocating for Congress to pass civil rights legislation protecting LGBTQ Americans and federalize the right to an abortion — two issues where he's changed his views after taking more conservative stances during his early years in public office.

When asked about Jackson's history with reproductive rights, Democratic state Sen. Stacy Brenner argued that it wasn't a deterrent in supporting him.

"What I find compelling about legislators and policymakers is when they are able to evolve with the thinking of where their heart is, where their mind is, when they learn about data and when they hear stories [from] their constituents," said Brenner, who also has a background as a farmer and nurse.

"That's what's happened for Troy," she added.

Jackson supporters celebrate his lengthy tenure in Maine politics as well as his blue-collar roots. And despite recent reporting in The Washington Post and CNN describing Jackson as exhibiting a short temper with colleagues during his time in office, he has faced minimal public pushback from state leaders in the lead-up to the convention.

A tough road ahead for the nominee

While Collins has faced competitive challengers before, Democrats see the fifth-term incumbent as particularly vulnerable this year. She's running in a state carried by Kamala Harris in 2024, and at a moment when many voters have soured on President Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran.

Still, even if Jackson is able to claim the nomination, he will face a difficult path to victory, with only about 100 days before voting ends on Nov. 3 to build up a war chest and make his case to voters.

In Collins, he would be facing off against one of the most senior Republican incumbents in the Senate. Collins, who has held her seat for 30 years, holds a massive fundraising edge, reporting $11 million in cash on hand, according to latest Federal Election Commission filings.

But Jackson's campaign argues that it has momentum, reporting a fundraising haul of more than $1 million since he announced his run.

"This campaign is powered by people who are sick of watching billionaires and corporations buy influence while working families get screwed," Jackson said in a statement Wednesday.

"Together, we're building the grassroots movement it will take to defeat Susan Collins and give Maine a senator who answers to working people."
news.summary: Democrats are hoping to move past Platner's scandal-plagued campaign as they look to unseat Republican incumbent Susan Collins. The apparent front-runner is former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson.

news.title: The art of the bluff? A look at Trump as negotiator in chief, from Iran to China
news.text:
WASHINGTON – Call it the art of the bluff.

Bombing Iran back to the Stone Age. Threatening to double the cost of Chinese imports. Filing multibillion-dollar lawsuits.

President Donald Trump storms ahead when embarking on a new policy or seeking to intimidate an adversary. But agreements often come after he trims his sails.

The commander-in-chief called Iranian leaders “very smart people, very good negotiators” after hammering out a framework for peace that later fell apart. He touted a “fantastic” trade deal that came after meeting with the “great leader,” China’s President Xi Jinping. And he settled lawsuits for fractions of a percent of what he’d demanded – or for the promise of avoiding tax audits.

More: Trump criticizes politicians, comedians at White House press dinner

It’s a strategy Trump learned in the bare-knuckle world of New York real estate development.

“I went in and asked for the world – for an unprecedented tax abatement – on the assumption that even if I got cut back, the break might still be sufficient,” Trump wrote in his 1987 book “Trump: The Art of the Deal.” “In a funny way, it was like a high stakes poker game in which neither side has very strong cards so both are forced to bluff.”

Here’s a look at how he’s deployed the approach as president.

Iran flips from 'Stone Ages' to 'very smart people' back to 'scum'

Trump’s comments on Iran have ranged from the bellicose to the complimentary.

Trump demanded “UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER!” in a March 6 post. He said in an April 1 post “we are blasting Iran into oblivion or, as they say, back to the Stone Ages!!!” And he said “A whole civilization will die tonight” in an April 7 post.

U.S. and Iranian officials signed a framework June 17 to stop the bombing, halt the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping in exchange for Tehran’s commitment not to develop nuclear weapons.

“They're very smart people, very good negotiators,” Trump said.

But after Iran resumed firing on commercial ships in the strait, Trump returned to the harsh talk. He told reporters at a NATO summit that Iranian leaders are “scum” and “sick people.”

“Honestly, they haven’t seen anything yet,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on July 21. “We’ve been nice.”

China tariff talks range from 'extremely hostile' to 'very friendly'

As the American eagle battled the Chinese dragon over trade, Trumps imposed tariffs on imports from China last year that threatened to reach 157% against “an extraordinarily aggressive” and “extremely hostile” position.

“I don’t think that’s sustainable for them,” he said.

But Trump repeatedly postponed or withdrew tariffs as he negotiated a trade agreement in October with the United States' third-largest trading partner.

"I think it was a very friendly meeting,” Trump said in reaching an agreement with Xi. “It was a good meeting for two very large, powerful countries. That's the way we should get along with a large powerful country.”

Despite the haggling, the government is collecting much more in tariffs under Trump. The average tariff rate for all imports is about 9%, according to the Tax Policy Center. Tariffs averaged 2.5% in 2024, the year before Trump’s second term, according to the Tax Foundation.

“I think the president has viewed tariffs as an opening salvo,” Dave Townsend, a partner at Dorsey & Whitney representing foreign clients in trade litigation, told USA TODAY.

Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics at the libertarian Cato Institute, said threatening higher amounts and eventually settling for less still left tariffs nearly four times higher than when Trump returned to office.

“In the trade space, Trump’s strategy is always maximalist at first, very public, very much trying to get everyone to overreact and then settling for what he actually wanted and having the temperature actually go down because everyone expected the worst,” Lincicome told USA TODAY. “There is some measure of relief when the worst doesn’t happen, even if you’re worse off.”

Trump warns of China election meddling but then acknowledges US does too

Another clash arose July 16, when Trump released a batch of declassified intelligence documents and accused China of trying to undermine the 2020 election. But a few days later, he downplayed the threat and said both countries meddle with each other.

Trump accused China of stealing 220 million voter files from states across the country in what he called “the largest compromise of election data in history,” although election experts said states sell the information.

Trump also said during that primetime televised speech that China sought to influence U.S. business leaders to "turn against" the president during his first term and paid reporters to write negatively about him.

"The Chinese government wanted (the) U.S. president to lose the next election, and the reason they wanted me to lose is because they knew I was wise to them," Trump said.

But when reporters asked July 21 about consequences for China, Trump downplayed the threat by suggesting the U.S. government does similar things to them.

"Well, we'll talk to them about it. It took place a long time ago," Trump told reporters the Oval Office. "I think China's maybe a little bit different today than it was then. But look, they do things. And we do things to them. I'll be honest. We do things to them, too. It's not a one-way street."

Trump shrugs off Supreme Court losses after promoting their significance

Trump worked the refs at the Supreme Court for his priorities of imposing tariffs and restricting birthright citizenship, but then shrugged off losses in both cases.

Trump said in December that a ruling against him in the tariffs case would be the “biggest threat in history to United States National Security.”

“WE’RE SCREWED!” if the court overturns the tariffs, Trump added in a social media post Jan. 12.

But after the Feb. 20 decision, Trump acknowledged other paths to tariffs.

“Yes, I have another way of doing Tariffs, but it is far slower, and more laborious than what was just determined, in a close decision, to be ‘illegal’ or ‘unconstitutional,’ with three powerful, and highly accurate, dissents!” he said on social media May 10.

In another major loss at the high court, Trump argued the country “cannot live with the shackles of Birthright Citizenship,” which he said wasn’t economical or sustainable in a social media post June 11. He reinforced the importance of the case by becoming the first sitting president to attend an oral argument.

But after the court ruled against him on the final day of its term June 30, Trump said another decision released the same day was more important because it confirmed his power to remove the heads of independent agencies.

Regarding the birthright citizenship defeat, “we can easily make it up in Congress through Legislation,” Trump said in a social media post June 30.

Billion-dollar lawsuits settled for millions but still 'jaw-dropping'

Trump, who frequently went to court before being elected president, hasn’t let his day job keep him from filing multibillion-dollar lawsuits. But in several high-profile cases he settled for millions – less than two-tenths of a percent of his demands – or an agreement to avoid future tax investigations.

For example, Trump filed a lawsuit against ABC in March 2024 after George Stephanopoulos inaccurately said he was found liable for raping columnist E. Jean Carroll in her civil case against him. ABC agreed in December 2024 to pay $15 million to Trump’s presidential library and $1 million for his legal fees.

Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit in October 2024 over the editing of a “60 Minutes” interview on CBS with his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris. He settled in July 2025 for $16 million from CBS owner Paramount.

Trump has also sued the Wall Street Journal for $10 billion for writing about his relationship with accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein and the New York Times for $15 billion for “disparaging articles” during the 2024 campaign. But those cases are unresolved.

Lee Levine, a lawyer who has represented media clients for 35 years, said naming a big price in a lawsuit is common and not unique to Trump.

“Lawyers always put in their complaints outrageous dollar figures, usually just a function of how tired their fingers get in typing zeros at their computers,” Levine said.

The settlements have been wins for Trump even though the numbers are a fraction of what he sought.

But he said the multimillion-dollar settlements, which came before the cases were tested in court, reflected timidity of the media companies seeking to avoid getting on the president’s wrong side.

“The amounts of those settlements standing on their own are jaw-dropping,” Levine said.

Trump, his two older sons and his namesake business filed a $10 billion lawsuit in January against the Internal Revenue Service after a contractor leaked their tax returns to reporters. The lawsuit said the Trumps suffered “reputational and financial harm, public embarrassment” and “unfairly tarnished their business reputations.”

But Trump, who oversees the IRS as president, reached an agreement in May that the IRS wouldn’t audit him for past tax liabilities. The agreement also envisioned a nearly $1.8 billion fund to repay people investigated by the Justice Department, but Trump dropped the provision after a public outcry and a judge is reviewing the agreement.

“This lawsuit was not brought to vindicate rights; it was brought to manipulate the judicial process,” U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams wrote.

Trump sometimes settles for a single rather than try for home run

Some of Trump's lawsuits have yielded results. Tariffs are being recalibrated. But the evaluation of his foreign policy remains unresolved because the war with Iran grinds on.

In “The Art of the Deal,” Trump wrote about not getting too greedy in financial negotiations.

news.title: 'Maybe he's a racist' - Trump critical of James
news.text:
United States President Donald Trump said LeBron James might be "a racist" when asked if the basketball star is the "best ever" to play the sport.

James, 41, announced on Friday he is set to continue his glittering career with the Philadelphia 76ers.

When asked about the move in a White House news conference later, Trump explained why he believed Michael Jordan was the better player.

Jordan, 63, won six NBA titles with the Chicago Bulls in the 1990s and NBA Most Valuable Player (MVP) five times.

When asked whether Jordan or James was the "best ever", Trump said: "Michael Jordan is a guy that's a friend of mine. I play golf with him. He's a really good guy.

"I think LeBron is, maybe he's a racist, but maybe he doesn't like Trump. I don't know. I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way."

James, who has not responded to Trump's comment, has been a regular critic of Trump during his terms as president and endorsed Democratic candidates Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris when they ran against him.

In 2017 he referred to Trump as "a bum" following a row over invitations to the White House for NBA-winning teams.

James has won four NBA titles with the Miami Heat (twice), the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Los Angeles Lakers.

He has been named the league's MVP four times and is the NBA's all-time leader in points and games played.

James will be looking to secure a fifth title with the 76ers following his announcement on Friday that he is heading to Philadelphia.

They now boast the talents of James and All-Stars Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team," James said in a lengthy post on social media.

news.title: James Talarico = Beto 0.5
news.text:
In a weird state, Houston is one of the weirder cities. It is deep, dark blue and has been for more than forty years, but it has had two Republican mayors, one in 1875 and one from 1978 - 1982. Its city council is predominantly Democrat. Harris County, where Houston is located, is one of the few counties in Texas that went for Kamala Harris in 2024. You can see it on a map of which counties voted for whom. A tiny spot of blue surrounded by red. Houston has also contributed its share of dingbats to Congress: Al Green (D-Texas), Shelia Jackson Lee (D-Texas), and Sylvester Turner (D-Texas). Houston is blue; people vote Democrat. It should be a walk in the park for any Democrat to campaign in Houston, right? 

Usually, yes. There’s always an exception to the rule, and that exception is James Talafreakco (Hat tip to Jesse Watters for that), uh, Talarico. The Democrats' best attempt at a serious Senate candidate is Mr. Lily White himself, aka Beto 0.5. It will amuse me till my dying day that the Democrats acted just like Democrats of old and bounced the black woman in favor of a white man. The chef’s kiss is that the black woman, Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), doesn’t blame the Democrats. She blames everyone else! 

Talarico came to Houston on July 19 to campaign for the Senate seat he is hoping to win. He spoke at the Kingdom Builders Center in southwest Houston. The area where the center is located is a lower-middle-class, working-poor area, with lots and lots of Democrats, lots of black Democrats. The people that Talarico needs in order to win. Everything started well; Talarico was greeted with applause and cheers, waving campaign signs and chanting “Take Back Texas." He spoke for 90 minutes, answered a wide variety of questions, and people appeared to be accepting his stance on the issues. 

It was when the last question was presented to Talarico that the problems appeared. Kandice Webber, 50, black, a resident of Houston and connected to the Houston chapter of Black Lives Matter, stood and said, “Our people don’t trust you for this reason, and you cannot win without us. So you stay here and you answer our questions, or you suffer the consequences.” Apparently, 90 minutes was not enough for Webber. 

When Talarico attempted to smooth things over by saying he appreciated her being there, she told him, “I came for my people, not for you.” Which set the assembled crowd to murmuring. Making another attempt to lower the tension, Talarico said, “It’s all right, it’s all right, it’s all right. This is what this conversation is supposed to be about.” He went on to answer other questions, but Webber was not happy and appeared visibly disappointed. 

Therein lies the major problem Talarico faces. Can he convince enough black voters that he’s a serious candidate and that he will make black voters' lives better if he wins the Senate seat? Is it possible? If he can’t, he loses, plain and simple. The Democrats have relied on the black vote for decades. They learned long ago that if they get enough black people voting for them, they can pretty much do whatever they want once they’re in office. Look at Los Angeles and Chicago and Detroit if you don’t think that’s true. 

However, some Democrats can schmooze better than others. Talarico appears not to have that ability yet. He may develop it more as the campaign grinds on, but if he has problems in a solidly Democratic stronghold such as Houston, then what does that say about the rest of the state? He was elected as a state representative, but all that means is that he was able to convince one specific section of the state that he was their guy. It is vastly different when you try to convince a state the size of Texas, the second most populous state in the U.S., that you’ll represent everyone properly. That is not what black Democratic voters want. They want someone who will listen to them and only them. Should Talarico win, will he? If he does, which is assumed, will he be able to get anything done? That remains largely to be seen. Should he win, he will be the junior Senator from Texas, with no power to do much of anything. The Senate is like the House of Representatives in that it is seniority-based. The longer you’re there, the more power you have. Will the black voters who put him there be willing to wait for him to collect the needed power? Again, that remains to be seen. 

The other matter that needs to be considered is the group who voted for his opponent, Crockett. As noted earlier, the black woman got pushed to the side for the white man. While Crockett did endorse Talarico after she lost, she has been completely absent from anything having to do with his campaign, to the point of claiming that the race she lost was racist and rigged against her. This does not surprise anyone. Crockett is a typical black Democrat. Everything is racist. EVERYTHING! Had Crockett decided to help Talarico by going on campaign stops with him, he would be farther along with the blacks that voted for her. As it is, there are a lot of blacks who are not happy with who won the primary, and they are making themselves known, like Webber did at the Houston campaign stop. Research on Webber does not say who she voted for in the primary, but it’s a pretty good guess that it wasn’t the white guy. 

Not to put too fine a point on it, Talarico needs the black vote, probably more than any other Democratic Party candidate in this election year. He needs it, he knows he needs it, but aside from throwing money at it — $25 million spent on black voter outreach — he doesn’t quite know what to do to get it. All the black voters have to do is stay home. All they have to do is not vote, and Talarico’s Senate hopes will crash faster than a two-year-old coming off a sugar high. He knows that, too, which probably keeps him up at night more than anything else.

news.title: Trump administration admits canceling grants based on politics
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has acknowledged in court documents that it canceled $7.6 billion in grants for hundreds of clean energy projects “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state” — in this case, 16 states that voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

The statement contradicts repeated assertions by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and other officials that the projects were canceled because they did not adequately advance the nation’s energy needs or had other problems that made them a poor investment of taxpayer dollars.

Democrats and environmental groups seized on the court filing Friday, saying the administration had “weaponized” the federal government to kill good jobs and punish working families because of their political views.

Democrats say what was ‘obvious’ has now been acknowledged

“This administration has now admitted in court what has long been obvious: it terminated nearly 300 cost-cutting energy projects for no reason other than the fact that the states they were in did not vote for the president in the 2024 election,” said Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio and Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state. Both are high-ranking Democrats on the House and Senate Appropriations committees, respectively.

“Weaponizing the federal government like this is outright un-American, and it’s hardworking families already struggling with sky-high costs who are suffering the consequences of this corrupt abuse of power,” Kaptur and Murray said.

They called on congressional Republicans to join them in holding the Trump administration “accountable for the President’s failure to look out for all Americans.”

The Energy Department announced last October that 321 funding awards across 223 projects were terminated, saying that after review, they “did not adequately advance the nation’s energy needs or were not economically viable.”

The cuts, part of broader attacks from President Donald Trump on climate programs and clean energy funding, slashed federal support for projects to build battery plants, develop hydrogen technology, upgrade the electric grid and capture carbon dioxide emissions.

Russell Vought, the White House budget director, highlighted the cutbacks in a social media post, saying money “to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being cancelled.”

The Energy Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Projects from many states were cut

Projects that were cut were located in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont and Washington state. All 16 targeted states supported Harris, but Wright said the cuts were “business decisions” based on whether the projects were a good use of taxpayer money or not.

The cuts were immediately challenged in court, and more than two dozen Democratic members of Congress, led by California Sens. Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla and Rep. Zoe Lofgren, wrote a letter to the Energy Department’s acting inspector general requesting a formal investigation. The department’s internal watchdog launched an investigation in December.

Government lawyers had p reviously confirmed in a court filing late last year that the selection of grants in fact “was influenced by whether a grantee’s address was located in a State that tends to elect ... Democratic candidates in state and national elections (so-called “Blue States”).”

That filing came in a separate suit filed by clean energy groups and the city of St. Paul, Minnesota, over the canceled funding. The most recent admission came in a case called Thakur v. Trump that’s been ongoing since last spring. news.title: ‘Maybe he’s a racist’: Trump critical of LeBron James
news.text:

James has won four NBA titles with the Miami Heat (twice), the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Los Angeles Lakers.

He has been named the league's MVP four times and is the NBA's all-time leader in points and games played.

James will be looking to secure a fifth title with the 76ers following his announcement on Friday that he is heading to Philadelphia.

news.title: Federal officials admit to withholding grants from states just because they didn’t vote for Trump
news.text:
Donald Trump’s administration has admitted that it canceled a block of roughly $7.5 billion in Biden-era clean energy funding “based solely” on the fact the money was flowing to projects in Democratic-led states.

The cuts were not based on “any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor,” the Department of Energy conceded last week as part of early negotiations in a federal lawsuit from University of California researchers.

Instead, the grants were included on a list of cancellations announced in October “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State.” 

The department added that with one exception, 284 terminated grants were slated to fund projects in Democratic-led states or states that voted for Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024. The roughly 340 grants that survived the chopping block were “in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election” or had at least one Republican senator, according to court filings.

The admission set off anger on Capitol Hill.

“This Administration has now admitted in court what has long been obvious: it terminated nearly 300 cost-cutting energy projects for no reason other than the fact that the states they were in did not vote for the President in the 2024 election,” Democratic lawmakers wrote in a statement.

“This is an astounding admission that the President and his team corruptly abused their power to kill good jobs and punish hard-working families because of their political views,” they said.

The Independent has contacted the Energy Department for comment.

The striking admission follows the Trump administration’s previous claims that the cuts were not influenced by politics and were instead aimed at ensuring federal funds flowed to effective and reliable energy projects.

“President Trump promised to protect taxpayer dollars and expand America’s supply of affordable, reliable, and secure energy,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement in October. 

The Department of Energy added at the time that its review sought to “identify waste” and “safeguard taxpayer dollars.”

Elsewhere in the lawsuit, which was filed last year, the Trump administration admitted to using keywords related to diversity, gender, vaccine hesitancy, and COVID-19 to guide cuts that canceled nearly $2 billion in grants to the University of California. 

Around the time the energy grants were canceled, top Trump administration figures used highly partisan language to describe the effort, which was announced the same day as a government shutdown began. 

Russell Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, wrote on social media that “nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda is being cancelled.”

The following day, Trump, who moved to slash billions in funding for projects in Democratic states during the shutdown, shared a video on Truth Social depicting Vought as the Grim Reaper, soundtracked by a song that warned Democrats the administration was “gonna tie your hands.”

Secretary Wright has denied partisan politics influenced the funding review.

“No decisions were made on politics,” he testified to members of Congress last month. “I keep hearing that charge. It’s bull****. We’re going to say it a million times.”

A spokesperson for the department told The New York Times on Friday that the initial review of grants, which was later submitted to the White House for further consideration, was apolitical, and that the secretary’s testimony remained accurate.

The allegations of political favoritism in the federal funding process are somewhat ironic, given that the Biden administration’s landmark climate funding law steered investments and incentives towards largely Republican-held districts, a move that advocates hoped would ensure the Inflation Reduction Act proved politically durable.

Instead, Republicans in Congress have gutted the law.

Renewed scrutiny into the grant process comes as the Trump administration is pushing to give political appointees more authority to award federal grants, rather than the current expert-led, peer-review system used in many science- and defense-related opportunities.

“This proposed rule would essentially undermine that process by adding a layer of political review that could undo scientific recommendations for reasons that have nothing to do with science,” Heather Pierce. senior director of science policy at the Association of American Medical Colleges, recently told NPR of the proposal.
news.summary: The Trump administration previously claimed the funding cuts were meant to stop wasteful spending and were not influenced by politics

news.title: Universities are out, AI is in under new Trump plan for science funding
news.text:
A new White House blueprint for scientific research is drawing mixed reactions from Massachusetts scientists, with some praising its focus on innovation and others fearful it presages a shift away from the longstanding research partnership between the federal government and universities.

The 120-plus-page report, “Science: A New Golden Age,” released Tuesday, would drastically reshape the country’s approach to science funding by making large investments in artificial intelligence, robotics, and private-public partnerships. It also proposes additional spending in science and technology education, programs for early-career scientists, and backing unconventional ideas through a “golden ticket” program that rewards higher-risk research.

Those involved in industry partnerships on AI say the recommendations validate their work. Other scientists, however, raised concerns about changes they said could further kneecap a research system that has long been held up as a model around the world. 

“These folks in this administration have figured out ways to write stuff that kind of looks good on the surface if you skim it,” said Victor Ambros, a Nobel Prize winner and professor of natural sciences at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School. “But it’s cleverly designed to advance an agenda.”

Billed as “the first comprehensive rethinking of the U.S. science and technology enterprise in over 80 years,” the plan comes amid a broader push by the Trump administration to expand its efforts to slash federal funding for disfavored topics and academic institutions. In May, the administration proposed letting political appointees decide on research funding, mandating each grant and contract align with White House priorities, and allowing the executive branch to disregard external scientific reviews and end funding at will. 

On Friday, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had canceled more than 200 grants from the Energy Department last year solely because the recipient was located in a state that voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.

The new White House report aims to prioritize the “individual scientist over legacy institutions” and focus on fields such as the biological sciences — including genomics and neuroscience — quantum information science, and nuclear energy.

“What we are trying to do here is laying the groundwork for new methods of doing science and figuring out which ones can produce the greatest output for the American scientific community,” Michael Kratsios, director of the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy and author of the report, told lawmakers in a hearing on Wednesday.

But experts say moving away from funding university-based research would likely do more harm to scientific development than good. 

The Trump administration is trying to “replace a system that has worked to the envy of the world,” said Ambros, whose Nobel-winning research was funded by the National Institutes of Health. 

The new report is “not a renovation” of the system, he said. ”It’s a teardown.” 

The proposal appears to approach scientific research in the same way a private equity firm would a potential investment target, said Colette Delawalla, founder and chief executive of Stand Up for Science, an advocacy group. 

For instance, in a letter introducing the report, Kratsios wrote that federal research agencies should “evaluate their own performance as capital allocators, test new ways of making grants, and construct portfolios with the intentionality of a serious investor.”

Administration officials seem to be looking for areas where the most money might be made and where the “fat” can be cut, Delawalla said. 

Shifting funding from academic institutions to individuals doesn’t make sense, she added; Universities provide critical infrastructure and resources for researchers to conduct their work. 

“It’s like hiring Tom Brady and then not having a stadium for him to play in and not having a football,” she said.

Some experts worry the report will be followed by a federal budget request that shifts dollars away from universities and toward private companies.

“There’s winners and losers in every policy,” said Scott Delaney, cofounder of Grant Witness, which tracks terminated scientific research grants. “Universities are losers under this policy — like full stop.” 

Delaney noted Massachusetts, a leader in university-led scientific innovation, receives the most federal funding for science per capita. 

“Now, Massachusetts also has a very robust private sector, biotech sector, pharma,” he said. “I do think there’s reason to believe that some of those institutions would benefit.” 

Joanne Padrón Carney, chief government relations officer for the American Association for the Advancement of Science, said the impacts of the plan remain unclear. 

“This report proposes an untested experiment on a national scale to reshape the innovation ecosystem,” Carney said in an email. “As with any experiment, it could yield results that are difficult to predict or create damage that could take decades to address.” 

‘AI revolution’

To prepare for an “AI revolution,” the administration calls for integrating AI into every stage of the scientific process, from drug discovery to analyzing data at NASA. Kratsios also announced a new $5 billion commitment from the federal government to make that happen, funding the administration’s so-called Genesis Mission.

Sam Scarpino did not read the report as a threat to funding at Northeastern University, where he’s the executive director of the Institute for Experiential AI. If anything, Kratsios’s vision validates the work he does, he said.

Scarpino and his team work with companies to both deploy and develop new AI tools with human oversight.

“Artificial intelligence is something of an existential moment for universities, and I think a report like this maybe gives some confidence that we’re heading in a reasonable direction,” Scarpino said

To him, the road map sketched by Kratsios leads to an “integrated, diversified research ecosystem” that includes both private sector businesses and universities, without one coming at the expense of the other.

“If we frame this report as that, it is very positive,” he said.

At Boston University, Gianluca Stringhini has received funding from OpenAI to conduct research in artificial intelligence focused on cybersecurity. His work seems to embody the exact model Kratsios is promoting. 

But partnerships between industry and academia only work with adequate support for both, said Stringhini. He is worried by recent funding cuts to scientific research and said most ideas that can be brought to market, such as his partnership with OpenAI, have been the product of years of academic inquiry. In an academic lab, his team has time to test new models and scrutinize results. Inherently, that takes time.

“It’s good to look at industry partnerships and something else than basic traditional academic research. But there needs to be basic academic research as well,” he said. “Otherwise, it is kind of a house of cards, and everything will fall apart.”

news.title: Trump admin admits terminating grants only in states that voted for Kamala Harris
news.text:

“All such grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election or has at least one Republican-caucusing Senator.”

“Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being cancelled. More info to come from [DOE],” Vought wrote. 

Democrats contend the filing demonstrates that Trump administration officials “corruptly abused their power” to terminate grants solely on the basis of the political identity of the states receiving federal money.

Patty Murray (D-Wash.), the vice chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio), the ranking member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Energy and Water Development, said in a joint statement. 

“This is an astounding admission that the president and his team corruptly abused their power to kill good jobs and punish hard-working families because of their political views,” they added. 

The lawmakers further fumed that Energy Secretary Chris Wright “swore up and down for months that these project terminations had absolutely nothing to do with politics, and now his lawyers are declaring that, in fact, politics was the only consideration.” 

A spokesperson for the Department of Energy told the New York Times that “there is no contradiction” between Wright’s testimony to Congress and the court filing. 

“Weaponizing the federal government like this is outright un-American, and it’s hardworking families already struggling with sky-high costs who are suffering the consequences of this corrupt abuse of power,’ the Democratic pols continued. 

“It’s good that several courts have already ruled against the terminations, and it’s high time Republicans join us to hold this administration accountable for the president’s failure to look out for all Americans.”

The White House and Department of Energy did not respond to The Post’s requests for comment.
news.summary: Democrats contend the filing demonstrates that Trump administration officials “corruptly abused their power” to terminate grants solely on the basis of the political identity of the states receiving federal money.

news.title: The Manufactured 'Bipartisan' Push For An AI Kill Switch
news.text:
Authored by Jordan Schachtel via American Greatness,

The AI Kill Switch Act, introduced Thursday by Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), seeks to hand the government unprecedented authority to order private companies to throttle, suspend, or shut down products in "kill switch" fashion, purely on their own arbitrary determination, with fines up to $20 million a day. Behind this carefully staged rollout is a fanatical coalition that looks like a broad consensus, but it is mostly one funding network with an arsenal of astroturf organizations at its disposal.

The Lieu-Moran bill arrived with endorsements preloaded from five groups: the AI Policy Network, Americans for Responsible Innovation, ControlAI, the Future of Life Institute, and the Alliance for Secure AI. Five organizations may sound like a broad coalition, so let's pull the thread and explore the details.

Americans for Responsible Innovation is funded by Coefficient Giving. Coefficient Giving is the freshly rebranded Open Philanthropy, the vehicle for Facebook billionaire Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna's fortune and the central bank of the far-left Effective Altruism (EA) movement's AI doom apparatus. Dustin Moskovitz was one of the largest individual megadonors supporting Kamala Harris's 2024 presidential election effort, contributing roughly $38 million to the pro-Harris super PAC Future Forward (FF PAC). The Open Philanthropy Action Fund pumped $2.9 million into ARI. ARI's 501(c)(3) sister organization collected another $3 million in general support.

The Alliance for Secure AI is the group built to make all this palatable to the Right. It spent six figures on ads running on Fox News and Newsmax last summer, pitching AI fear to conservative audiences. Who pays for the conservative outreach? In May, the New York Times reported that the Alliance for Secure AI is funded by ... Coefficient Giving. Surprise! You will search its website for that disclosure in vain.

ControlAI, the third member, openly advocates an international prohibition on advanced AI development and swims in the same donor waters. The group's top leaders have been calling for a complete shutdown of AI development since the very early iterations of ChatGPT.

The Future of Life Institute, which has also received millions from Coefficient Giving, is an EA-aligned leftist nonprofit best known for its ruthless insistence that America must force industry to "pause AI" indefinitely.

The AI Policy Network (AIPN) is an AI doomer outfit that is supported by leftist tech bros in Silicon Valley, some of whom are longtime AI panic mongers and influential executives at Anthropic and OpenAI.

This power grab arrives on the heels of the OpenAI sandbox episode, in which the company itself reported a security breach that has not been independently verified. OpenAI has every incentive to inflate the dangers of its own product because a frightening "autonomous" AI is both a better marketing pitch and a better argument for the regulatory moat that keeps its future competitors out. Washington is now being asked to hand a cabinet secretary sweeping authority over private enterprise on the strength of an incident report written by the party that stands to benefit.

So the "broad coalition" is substantially one checkbook, belonging to a left-wing Silicon Valley billionaire, laundered through a series of organizations that act as window dressing for one agenda. This is not bipartisanship, but rather the lobbyist-concocted appearance of bipartisanship.

The bill empowers the Homeland Security secretary with a shutdown trigger that includes a loss-of-control scenario, defined to cover a model behaving contrary to instructions in "another high-stakes context." That phrase is defined nowhere. The company must comply immediately without recourse. Its petition for reconsideration, the statute says flatly, does not stay the order. If the secretary ignores the petition for five days, silence counts as a denial. Court review would, of course, come months later, long after the product went dark, the business was likely destroyed, and all of the customers went elsewhere. Do we really want to grant the government this power?

And the definitions of who is covered? Rewritten by the agency, by rule, every single year, guided by a factor list that ends with "such other factors as the secretary determines relevant." Try executing a successful business strategy when your legal exposure gets redefined annually by government bureaucrats.

Some frontier AI model companies are not yet protesting the bill, largely because this enormous compliance burden could potentially create a wall around the incumbents. The giants can absorb the lawyers, the audits, the whims, and the like. Startups that attempt to catch up could get obliterated in one fell swoop. This kind of regulation is deliberately priced at a level only the largest firms can bear. It is a moat with a safety label.

The AI doomer lobby wants its federal chokepoint, and some of its frontier lab collaborators get a licensing wall between themselves and their future competitors. Everyone in this somewhat complex coalition wins except the American innovators.

What Congress is being sold is a federal "kill switch" button for upstart private enterprise, wielded on undefined standards and immune to timely challenges; and it's all being pushed by a fake "movement" that is mostly one billionaire's philanthropic arm.

Jordan Schachtel is an independent journalist who covers AI, tech, and world politics, and he's the publisher of The Dossier on Substack.

news.title: Trump administration concedes that it canceled research grants in blue states
news.text: The Trump administration admitted that it terminated nearly 300 federal research grants “solely because” the projects were connected to states that voted against President Donald Trump in 2024 and had two Democratic senators in office, according to court filings. In the filing, the administration wrote as an undisputed statement of fact that on a list of more than 2,300 financial assistance awards across the Department of Energy, 624 grants on these lists were designated either “termination” or “cancel.” Of those 624 grants, Jeff Novak, the principal deputy general counsel of the Department of Energy, wrote that in October 2025 the Office of Management and Budget identified 284 specific grants that were marked to be terminated. Novak wrote that with one exception, “the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators.” Novak added that the remaining 340 grants proposed for termination were ultimately not canceled in October 2025 nor since then. “All such grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to President Trump in the 2024 election or has at least one Republican-caucusing Senator,” Novak wrote of the unterminated grants. Novak wrote that the decision to cancel the grants listed in the October notice tranche — those 284 — was not “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction, or performance-based factor.” “DOE accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state, i.e., whether the recipient’s location and/or place of performance was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State,” Novak wrote. He added that the Department of Energy “will not contend that it looked beyond the prime grantee(s) to consider the political identity or geographic distribution of downstream beneficiaries of the grant funds.” The New York Times first reported this filing. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Department of Energy argued in a statement Friday that court filings did not show that termination decisions were made on a political basis. “That is a misrepresentation of the court filing and of Mr. Novak’s words,” Ben Dietderich, press secretary for the Energy Department, said in a statement. “None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations. Secretary Wright has explained this numerous times in briefings on Capitol Hill.” In an appearance before the House Science, Space and Technology Committee in June, Energy Secretary Chris Wright denied that decisions made around grant cancellations were partisan. “No decisions were made on politics. I keep hearing that charge. It’s bulls---t. We’re going to say it a million times,” Wright said. In a social media post in October, when the 284 grants were canceled, OMB Director Russ Vought wrote, “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being cancelled.” Vought listed 16 states where projects were canceled, including California, New York, Colorado, Vermont and New Jersey, among others. The filing comes as the Office of Management and Budget proposed a new rule that would allow political appointees to gain unprecedented control over the $1 trillion per year that is provided by federal grants. The office argues that the rule is meant to ensure that grants align with the sitting president’s priorities and to improve oversight. The rule proposes that political appointees screen grant applications to ensure they do not “promote anti-American values,” and they could terminate grants they saw as “no longer in the Federal Government’s interest.” The 284 federal grants canceled by the Department of Energy are just one sect of funding that has been targeted by the Trump administration. Since Trump began his second term, the administration has canceled grants for including mentions of DEI and has frozen research funding at universities like Harvard based on allegations of antisemitism. Trump has also threatened to pull funding from states that do not conform to his policies. In January, he said he would deny federal funding to states that resisted his anti-immigration agenda and had so-called sanctuary cities.

news.title: Democrats approve new primary election calendar, putting South Carolina first
news.text:
South Carolina was chosen to hold the first Democratic presidential primary in 2028 after a panel voted on the calendar Friday afternoon. The move was pushed by key Democrats to prioritize Black voters, a reliable and influential voting bloc for the party.

The Democratic National Committee's Rules and Bylaws panel recommended South Carolina vote first over Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa, who had each been seeking the first spot. Only six states will be permitted to hold primaries before Super Tuesday on March 7, 2028.

The order recommended by the panel is South Carolina's primary, to be held on Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada and New Hampshire, which are typically early voting states. New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia would also be permitted to hold early contests. This calendar will be presented to the full DNC in August, to be voted on and finalized.

South Carolina and the other five states could now hold early nominating contests, a play they have been pushing for since the start of this year. 

During the committee meeting Friday some states' party leaders and allies were making cases for why their state should go early.

"The place to start is in the West," said David McDonald, a member of the committee, "The place to start is in Nevada, which offers the best combination of diversity, certainty and opportunity."

McDonald was likely referring to Nevada's diverse population of Latino, Black, Asian American and Pacific Islander, Native American and working class voters.

Nevada was considered alongside South Carolina because the party also wants to prioritize Latino voters, a voting group that had a significant election impact in 2024 when President Trump won reelection. Because 2028 is an open primary, advocates for these two states argue they give candidates the best chance to be tested by influential voting blocs. At the end, some members raised concerns about Nevada being able to rapidly process election results.

South Carolina previously led the Democratic presidential primary in 2024 — the first time the process didn't start with the Iowa caucuses and New Hampshire's primary election. Some members of the panel spoke about the southern state's role in former President Joe Biden's 2020 nomination. Biden picked up his first early state victory in South Carolina that year, before winning other southern states on Super Tuesday. 

Nearly one in four registered voters in South Carolina is Black, according to state voting data. According to AP Vote Cast, 83% of Black voters nationwide backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in the last presidential election.

"The South is not the past, we are the future," said Christale Spain, chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party. "And if we are serious about changing this country, Democrats have to start winning in the South."

Spain said Democrats need to demonstrate that they are serious about making the investment in the South, adding that South Carolina has a lot of flexibility for its election dates and two weeks of early voting.

South Carolina allies said that the party should show that Black voters are a priority for them in a year when the Supreme Court's Voting Rights Act decision led to multiple states drawing new Congressional boundaries in districts that had previously ruled in violation of that law.

The six states picked to be first together tell the story of who the Democratic party is, said Debbie Dingell, a congresswoman from Michigan, urging members to not read too much into who was given the first slot. Michigan will also vote early in the current plan.
news.summary: Democrats chose South Carolina for the first 2028 presidential primary, then Nevada, prioritizing Black and Latino voters. New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia also hold early contests.

news.title: President Trump Speculates LeBron James Is a ‘Racist’ After Shocking 76ers Signing
news.text:
President Donald Trump has weighed in on the NBA GOAT debate, and he prefers Michael Jordan over LeBron James, who he speculates might be racist.
Trump, 80, was asked about the long-held basketball argument on Friday, July 24, shortly after James, 41, announced that he would sign with the Philadelphia 76ers.
“Michael Jordan’s a guy that’s a friend of mine,” Trump said. “I play golf with him. He’s a really good guy.”
He then added, “And I think LeBron, maybe he’s a racist. But maybe he doesn't like Trump. I don't know. I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way."
It is not clear what Trump was referring to when he questioned if James might be racist.
James has been an outspoken detractor of Trump throughout both of his terms as President. He endorsed Hillary Clinton in 2016, saying she was better equipped to make sure kids didn’t “fall through the cracks.”
“When I look at this year’s presidential race, it’s clear which candidate believes the same thing,” he said at the time. “Only one person running truly understands the struggles of an Akron child born into poverty. And when I think about the kinds of policies and ideas the kids in my foundation need from our government, the choice is clear. That candidate is Hillary Clinton.”
He also endorsed former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris in each of their campaigns against Trump.
“What are we even talking about here??” he wrote via X the week before the 2024 election. “When I think about my kids and my family and how they will grow up, the choice is clear to me. VOTE KAMALA HARRIS!!!”
In 2020, when Trump said he turned off an NBA game after seeing players kneel for the national anthem, James said, "I really don't think the basketball community are sad about losing his viewership, him viewing the game. And that’s all I got to say.”
Jordan, for his part, has famously stayed out of politics throughout his career and does not publicly endorse candidates for office.
He angered Democrats in 1990 when he refused to endorse the party’s candidate in a North Carolina senate race when he said “Republicans buy shoes too.” (Jordan, 63, and Nike launched Jordan Brand six years before, kickstarting arguably the most successful athlete-brand partnership of all-time.)
In ESPN’s 2020 documentary, The Last Dance, which detailed Jordan’s final season with the Chicago Bulls, Jordan reflected on the comment, which he said was made “in jest.”
“It was thrown off the cuff. My mother asked to do a PSA for [Democratic candidate] Harvey Gantt, and I said, 'Look, Mom, I'm not speaking out of pocket about someone that I don't know. But I will send a contribution to support him.' Which is what I did.”

news.title: Trump officials admit targeting Democratic states for grant cuts
news.text:
WASHINGTON >> When the Trump administration canceled more than $7.5 billion in Biden-era federal grants for clean energy projects in October, it framed the move as an urgent corrective to protect taxpayer funds from waste.

But it wasn’t true.

In little-noticed court documents, federal officials acknowledged this month that they had terminated the funding “based solely” on political criteria, targeting projects in states that were represented by Democrats and had voted for Kamala Harris, the party’s presidential nominee, in the 2024 election.

The stunning admission offered an unvarnished glimpse into the way President Donald Trump has weaponized the provision of federal education, energy, health, housing and infrastructure aid in his second term. Far from rooting out the sort of misspending that Trump sees as rife in Washington, the White House has instead sought to leverage the budget as a tool to assist its allies — or as a cudgel to hurt the president’s foes.

>> RELATED STORY: Hawaii joins lawsuit over Trump election conditions on disaster aid

The saga illustrates the stakes as the Trump administration is completing a set of rules that would provide the president even greater control over more than $1 trillion in annual federal grants. To critics, the new regulation would only make it easier for Trump to strike wider tranches of congressionally approved funding over political differences.

“The risk that the Trump administration is willing to go to extreme lengths to politicize grant-making is not a hypothetical,” said Devin O’Connor, a senior fellow at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning group. He previously served at the White House budget office under former President Joe Biden.

“If they are willing to be that blatant about it,” O’Connor said of the court filing, “then I think we should take seriously when they put forward a framework that would allow for the extreme politicization of grant-making across all of the federal government.”

The White House and the Energy Department did not respond to requests for comment.

The administration’s latest concession about the grants came in a lawsuit filed by a group of California researchers challenging various federal agencies that have canceled Biden-era funding.

After reviewing its spending, the Energy Department last fall created a list that recommended canceling more than 600 grants awarded by the Biden administration for a wide range of novel energy projects. That list included funding for projects in states represented by both Republicans and Democrats.

But in October, the White House budget office, led by Russell Vought, terminated only 284 of those grants. In a social media post announcing the news, Vought pointed to the motivations: “Nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left’s climate agenda is being canceled,” he said.

Months later, in court filings, federal officials indicated there was little else that had informed the final decision about which grants to cancel.

“With one exception,” a lawyer for the Energy Department conceded in a court filing this month, “the 284 terminated grants had a recipient location and/or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing senators.”

The lawyer acknowledged that none of the grants were included in the October terminations “based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor.”

In contrast, the administration left untouched hundreds of additional energy grants in states that were represented by Republicans and had backed Trump in the last election, even though the Energy Department had recommended canceling them, the government confirmed in the July court filing.

The cancellations coincided with a broader White House effort at the time to pressure Democratic lawmakers to cave in a fight over funding that had shut down the government. That month, Trump had vocalized the strategy: He threatened openly to slash what he described as “Democrat agencies,” while Vought announced a series of additional spending cuts targeting other Democratic-led states.

As a result, the administration’s actions halted funding for hundreds of energy projects, including upgrades to electrical grids in states such as California and Oregon; efforts to reduce methane leaks from oil and gas operations in Colorado; and large hubs to produce clean-burning hydrogen fuels in California and the Pacific Northwest. Some awardees later sued the Trump administration in an effort to restore their grants.

Federal officials offered the new details about the grant cancellations as part of an agreement with plaintiffs meant to spare the government an exhaustive, evidence-uncovering process known as discovery, the court filings said. That process could have required federal agencies to hand over more damaging records.

The agreement applied to other federal agencies targeted by the lawsuit, including the Department of Transportation and the Department of Health and Human Services. Some agencies later revealed new details about the ways in which they reviewed their grants — using specific keywords tied to Trump’s political priorities and past directives — for possible cancellations, according to additional court documents this month. Lawyers for the plaintiffs did not respond to a request for comment.

The filings also appeared to undermine the congressional testimony of Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who spoke about the cancellations in a June House hearing: “No decisions were made on politics.”

The Energy Department previously conceded in two other cases that politics had been a “primary reason” for the cancellations. In those cases, Amit P. Mehta, a judge in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, eventually ruled that the agency had improperly canceled more than a dozen grants. But the latest concession is far more detailed and sweeping, and it sparked new anger on Capitol Hill.

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the chamber’s appropriations committee, and Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, who leads her party on the House’s top energy appropriations panel, said in a joint statement on Friday that politically minded grant cuts amounted to an “outright un-American” weaponization of government.

“This administration has now admitted in court what has long been obvious: It terminated nearly 300 cost-cutting energy projects for no reason other than the fact that the states they were in did not vote for the president in the 2024 election,” they added. “This is an astounding admission that the president and his team corruptly abused their power to kill good jobs and punish hardworking families because of their political views.”

Many Democrats have raised those same concerns as the White House looks to assert even greater control over federal grants. Those proposed regulations, which are expected to be completed by October, would require Trump’s political appointees to review all federal grants, with the power to block or revoke money if they did not conform to administration priorities.

The White House has also sought to layer additional restrictions on grant recipients, limiting their political activities, memberships and even appearances at conferences, along with vague requirements that they cannot use the money for certain purposes, including those deemed “anti-American.”

The proposed rules have sparked widespread backlash from anti-poverty groups, arts practitioners, city leaders, law enforcement officials, scientists and others. These critics flooded the government with thousands of comments arguing that the measures could undermine crucial government services.

But the administration has maintained that the new rules would help to prevent waste and align federal spending with Trump’s priorities. Testifying at a congressional hearing this month, Vought said it would ensure “that we have democratic control of the spending that is going out.”

news.title: White House admits it scrapped grants to blue states because they didn’t vote for Trump
news.text:
During last fall’s government shutdown, the Trump administration started cutting energy grants to states, but the only states that were seriously affected were ones Donald Trump lost in the 2024 election. At the time, officials in the affected states accused the White House of “mafioso tactics” and brazenly abusing its powers by politicizing grant decisions that are supposed to be based on merit.

Team Trump was initially dismissive of the claims. Russell Vought, the White House budget director who terminated hundreds of grants, insisted that he was simply paring back Biden-era federal grants that the White House considered wasteful because as Vought put it, they were part of a “Green New Scam” — whatever that was supposed to mean.

It wasn’t long, however, before that posture started evolving.

In December, for example, the Republican administration’s lawyers made no real effort to deny the underlying allegations, instead arguing in a court filing that it’s “constitutionally permissible” to consider partisan politics when distributing (or canceling) federal funds.

This week, Team Trump gave up the game, effectively admitting in a legal filing that the “mafioso tactics” claims were correct all along. The New York Times reported:

In little-noticed court documents, federal officials acknowledged this month that they had terminated the funding “based solely” on political criteria, targeting projects in states that were represented by Democrats and had voted for Kamala Harris, the party’s presidential nominee, in the 2024 election.

The stunning admission offered an unvarnished glimpse into the way President Trump has weaponized the provision of federal education, energy, health, housing and infrastructure aid in his second term. Far from rooting out the sort of misspending that Mr. Trump sees as rife in Washington, the White House has instead sought to leverage the budget as a tool to assist its allies — or as a cudgel to hurt the president’s foes.

The White House and the Energy Department did not respond to the Times’ requests for comment, which is just as well, since I seriously doubt even the most creative Republican communications professionals could put a positive spin on developments like these.

The article went on to note, “Federal officials offered the new details about the grant cancellations as part of an agreement with plaintiffs meant to spare the government an exhaustive, evidence-uncovering process known as discovery, the court filings said. That process could have required federal agencies to hand over more damaging records.”

In other words, this is the good version of the developments from the White House’s perspective. The agreement reached by the administration prevented other potential abuses from coming to public light.

We’re talking about a White House that admits it withholds federal resources from states based on local voters casting ballots in ways the president doesn’t like. Not to put too fine a point on this, but that sounds an awful lot like an impeachable offense. It’s a fundamental corruption of how federal tax dollars are allocated.

Making matters worse is the familiarity of the circumstances. Team Trump approves disaster aid requests from red states, while rejecting comparable requests from blue states. Team Trump curtails healthcare funds, but only for states the White House doesn’t like. Team Trump launches a supposed crackdown on “fraud” in social insurance programs, but its sole focus is on Democratic cities and states.

Taking stock of the broader dynamic, the Times’ Jamelle Bouie argued last fall, “Trump seems to see Democratic-led states — and the people in them — less as constituents to which he has a set of larger obligations and more as enemies to be pacified and defeated. For Trump, there is no whole people of the United States. There are only his people and his states.”

The Republican White House seems unnervingly eager to prove the observation true.

This post updates our related earlier coverage.

news.title: Jon Ossoff's 2028 Chances Compared to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
news.text: Senator Jon Ossoff’s chances of winning the 2028 Democratic presidential primary surged past Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on prediction markets, as speculation about who could jump into the race continues. The 2028 presidential field could begin coming into view in the months ahead with candidates potentially announcing their campaigns as early as next year after the midterms. On the Democratic side, prospective candidates are already testing their messages and heading to key primary states to build up their name recognition and make inroads with voters. Ossoff, who represents Georgia in the U.S. Senate, has been named as a potential candidate as he runs for reelection this year. Although the first votes won’t be cast for more than a year, polls and prediction markets can signal which candidates have early momentum among the electorate. Donors and voters can use these early signals to gauge whether a candidate is viable, so the numbers matter to a candidate's ability to fundraise and garner media attention. They also measure initial name recognition of potential candidates. Newsweek reached out to Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez’s teams for comment via email. Jon Ossoff’s Chances Surge in Prediction Markets Ossoff has downplayed talk of a 2028 presidential run, but his chances have increased on prediction markets in recent weeks. On Friday, his chances rose to 16 percent, surpassing Ocasio-Cortez’s 14 percent on Polymarket. Only California Governor Gavin Newsom had a higher chance of winning the nomination at 20 percent. One month earlier, Ossoff had a 9 percent chance of winning the nomination; he had less than a 4 percent chance of winning at the start of the year on January 1, according to Polymarket. Former Vice President Kamala Harris had a 7 percent chance of winning, while former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro had a 5 percent chance. Ossoff’s chances have also increased on Kalshi, where he had a 16 percent chance of winning on Friday compared to Newsom’s 18 percent and Ocasio-Cortez’s 15 percent. What Latest Polling Shows About Democrats’ 2028 Chances A new Emerson College poll pointed to Buttigieg as the front-runner to win the nomination, with 19 percent saying they would vote for him, followed by Newsom at 17 percent. Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez each received 13 percent in that poll, while Harris polled at 8 percent. Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear received 7 percent, while Shapiro received 5 percent support. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker polled at 3 percent, while 2 percent said they would vote for California Representative Ro Khanna. An additional 13 percent said they were undecided about who they would support for the nomination. It surveyed 574 Democrats from July 19-20 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A McLaughlin poll found Harris leading with 28 percent support, followed by Newsom at 17 percent and Ocasio-Cortez at 10 percent. Eight percent backed Buttigieg, while Arizona Senator Mark Kelly received 7 percent support. Notably, Ossoff was not included in that poll. It surveyed 1,000 general election voters from July 15-21, 2026. Ossoff Running for Reelection in Swing State Georgia Ossoff has said he is not launching a White House bid, telling CNN, “I am not running for president in 2028; I have no interest in running for president in 2028.” He said he is “laser-focused” on winning reelection in Georgia this year in a race the Cook Political Report forecasts as Lean Democrat. He is currently running for reelection in Georgia, a critical battleground state that has become more competitive in recent elections. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball view the race as Lean Democrat as he faces a challenge from GOP Representative Mike Collins. A strong showing in this year's Senate race could fuel calls for him to run in 2028 as Democrats search for a candidate who can win in purple states. Some Democrats view Ossoff as a candidate who may be able to unite the party, which has faced divisions between the more progressive and moderate factions ahead of the midterms. A new independent poll of the race found Ossoff with a lead. Ossoff received support from 52 percent of respondents in the latest AARP poll, compared to Collins’ 43 percent. Five percent said they were undecided about who they would support. The poll was conducted on behalf of AARP by Fabrizio Ward, a Republican pollster, and Impact Research, a Democratic pollster. It surveyed 1,060 likely voters across Georgia from July 13-16, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Interviews were conducted on cellphones, landlines and SMS-to-web. What Potential 2028 Candidates Have Said About Running Some 2028 Democrats haven’t ruled out running. Harris, who has traveled to states like Michigan and South Carolina in recent months, suggested she could run again without making a formal announcement. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she told Reverend Al Sharpton in April after he asked whether she planned to run for president in 2028 during the National Action Network’s annual convention. Harris noted she “served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States.” “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office. I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires,” she said. Newsom discussed the possibility of running in a June 2025 interview with The Wall Street Journal. “I'm not thinking about running, but it's a path that I could see unfold,” he said. Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to President Barack Obama, in May. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating."
